rubric.description: Gives two further valid characteristics of a good hypothesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two additional distinct correct characteristics.

written.text: Define biodiversity.
modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms in a particular area or on Earth.
It includes genetic diversity, species diversity and ecosystem diversity.
written.followUp: Name the three levels at which biodiversity is commonly described.

rubric.why: Checks the core meaning of biodiversity.
rubric.description: Defines biodiversity as the variety of living organisms or life forms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the basic definition.

rubric.why: Checks recognition of the main levels of biodiversity.
rubric.description: Mentions genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for all three levels.

written.text: Write down two main aims of classification.
modelAnswer: Classification helps identify organisms.
It arranges organisms into groups, making them easier to study.
written.followUp: Give two reasons why classification is useful in the study of organisms.

rubric.why: Identifying organisms is one main aim of classification.
rubric.description: States that classification helps identify organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying organisms as an aim.

rubric.why: Grouping organisms makes them easier to study.
rubric.description: States that classification groups organisms to make their study easier.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that grouping makes organisms easier to study.

written.text: Differentiate between cristae and cisternae.
modelAnswer: Cristae are folds of the inner membrane of mitochondria.
Cisternae are flattened membranous sacs of the endoplasmic reticulum.
written.followUp: Differentiate between the inner and outer membranes of a mitochondrion.

rubric.why: Cristae are the folds of the mitochondrial inner membrane.
rubric.description: Defines cristae as folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct location and structure of cristae.

rubric.why: Cisternae are flattened membranous sacs, commonly described as parts of the endoplasmic reticulum.
rubric.description: Defines cisternae as flattened membranous sacs of the endoplasmic reticulum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct structure and location of cisternae.

written.text: Define facilitated diffusion.
modelAnswer: Facilitated diffusion is the passive movement of substances across a cell membrane from a higher concentration to a lower concentration.
The substances pass through channel or carrier proteins in the membrane, and no cellular energy is used.
written.followUp: What is simple diffusion, and how does it differ from facilitated diffusion?

rubric.why: Facilitated diffusion is passive movement down a concentration gradient.
rubric.description: States that substances move passively from higher to lower concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the passive, downhill movement.

rubric.why: Facilitated diffusion occurs through proteins in the cell membrane.
rubric.description: Identifies membrane channel or carrier proteins as the route of transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the membrane proteins involved.

written.text: Differentiate between disjunction and non-disjunction.
modelAnswer: In disjunction, chromosomes or chromatids separate and move to opposite poles during cell division.
In nondisjunction, they fail to separate properly, producing cells with abnormal chromosome numbers.
written.followUp: What happens to chromosome number when nondisjunction occurs during meiosis?

rubric.why: Disjunction is the normal separation of chromosomes during cell division.
rubric.description: States that chromosomes or chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the normal separation.

rubric.why: Nondisjunction is a failure of normal chromosome separation and can produce cells with abnormal chromosome numbers.
rubric.description: States that chromosomes fail to separate, causing abnormal chromosome numbers in the resulting cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the failure to separate and its consequence.

written.text: What is meant by apoptosis?
modelAnswer: Apoptosis is programmed, controlled cell death.
It removes damaged or unneeded cells from an organism.
written.followUp: Why is apoptosis important in the development and maintenance of an organism?

rubric.why: Apoptosis is the regulated process of cell death.
rubric.description: Defines apoptosis as programmed or controlled cell death.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition.

rubric.why: Apoptosis removes cells that are damaged or no longer needed.
rubric.description: States that apoptosis removes damaged or unnecessary cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct role of apoptosis.

written.text: What are enzymes?
modelAnswer: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts.
They speed up chemical reactions in living organisms.
written.followUp: What is an enzyme, and what role does it perform in a cell?

rubric.why: Identifies the biological nature of enzymes.
rubric.description: States that enzymes are proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying enzymes as proteins.

rubric.why: States the function that defines enzymes.
rubric.description: States that enzymes act as biological catalysts and speed up reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that enzymes catalyse or speed up biochemical reactions.

written.text: Define metabolism and describe its importance.
modelAnswer: Metabolism is the sum of all the chemical reactions taking place in an organism or its cells.
These reactions provide energy and materials needed for growth, repair, and maintenance of the body.
written.followUp: What is an enzyme, and what happens to it during the reaction it catalyses?

rubric.why: Defines metabolism as the totality of chemical reactions in the organism.
rubric.description: Defines metabolism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing metabolism as the sum or total of the chemical reactions occurring in an organism or its cells.

rubric.why: States why metabolism is essential for life.
rubric.description: Gives the importance of metabolism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking metabolism to obtaining energy or to growth, repair, or maintenance of the body.

written.text: Describe the effect of concentration of carbon dioxide at photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: As the concentration of carbon dioxide increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases, provided other factors are adequate.
The rate eventually levels off because another factor becomes limiting.
written.followUp: How does light intensity affect the rate of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Identifies the initial effect of increasing carbon dioxide concentration.
rubric.description: Explains that increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a rise in carbon dioxide concentration increases the photosynthetic rate, at least initially.

rubric.why: Recognises that carbon dioxide is not the only factor controlling photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Describes the limit to the effect of increasing carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate eventually levels off or reaches a maximum when another factor becomes limiting.

written.text: What is lactic acid fermentation?
modelAnswer: Lactic acid fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose, occurring when oxygen is unavailable.
It produces lactic acid and releases a small amount of energy.
written.followUp: What is alcoholic fermentation, and what are its products?

rubric.why: Identifies the process as an anaerobic breakdown of glucose.
rubric.description: States that lactic acid fermentation takes place without oxygen.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the process as anaerobic or stating that it occurs in the absence of oxygen.

rubric.why: Names the characteristic product of this type of fermentation.
rubric.description: Names lactic acid as the product of fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming lactic acid as a product; energy release may also be mentioned.

written.text: Describe the importance of anaerobic respiration (fermentation).
modelAnswer: When the oxygen supply to muscles is insufficient, anaerobic respiration releases some energy and produces lactic acid.
Fermentation by microorganisms is used in food production, for example in bread-making and brewing alcoholic drinks.
written.followUp: State one role of fermentation in food production and one situation in which it occurs in the human body.

rubric.why: Identifies fermentation as a way to release some energy when oxygen is insufficient.
rubric.description: States the role of fermentation in muscles when oxygen is limited.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that muscle cells can release energy by anaerobic respiration when oxygen is insufficient, producing lactic acid.

rubric.why: Gives a practical use of fermentation.
rubric.description: Gives an application of fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct use such as bread-making or producing alcoholic drinks.

written.text: Define pressure flow mechanism.
modelAnswer: The pressure flow mechanism is the movement of food through the phloem from a source to a sink due to a pressure difference.
Sugars loaded at the source cause water to enter the phloem, raising pressure; sap then flows towards the lower-pressure sink.
written.followUp: Explain how a pressure difference helps move sugars through the phloem.

rubric.why: Identifies the region where sugars enter the phloem and pressure rises.
rubric.description: Describes sugar loading at the source and the resulting rise in pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sugars are loaded into the phloem at the source, causing water to enter and pressure to rise.

rubric.why: Explains that a pressure difference drives movement towards the sink.
rubric.description: Defines pressure flow as movement of phloem sap down a pressure gradient from source to sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing movement from the high-pressure source towards the lower-pressure sink.

written.text: Describe cellular organizations of organisms, its two types.
modelAnswer: Organisms are classified by their cellular organization as unicellular or multicellular.
Unicellular organisms consist of a single cell, which carries out all life processes; examples include Amoeba and bacteria.
Multicellular organisms consist of many cells; examples include plants and animals.
In many multicellular organisms, cells are specialized to perform different functions.
written.followUp: Compare unicellular and multicellular organisms, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Describes the first type of cellular organization and its basic feature.
rubric.description: Describes unicellular organisms.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for stating that a unicellular organism consists of one cell, and 1 for a correct example such as Amoeba, a bacterium, or yeast.

rubric.why: Describes the second type and distinguishes its organization from that of unicellular organisms.
rubric.description: Describes multicellular organisms.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for stating that a multicellular organism consists of many cells, and 1 for a correct example such as a plant or animal. Credit may be given for noting that its cells are specialized.

written.text: Write a comprehensive note on nucleus.
modelAnswer: The nucleus is usually a prominent organelle in the cell and is surrounded by a double nuclear membrane with pores.
It contains nucleoplasm, in which the nucleolus and chromatin are present.
Chromatin contains DNA and forms chromosomes during cell division; genes on DNA carry hereditary information.
The nucleus controls the activities of the cell and transmits hereditary information.
written.followUp: Describe the structure of the nucleus and state its main functions.

rubric.why: Describes the boundary of the nucleus and how it communicates with the cytoplasm.
rubric.description: Describes the nuclear envelope.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks: 1 for stating that the nucleus is surrounded by a double nuclear membrane or envelope, and 1 for mentioning pores in it.

rubric.why: Identifies important contents of the nucleus.
rubric.description: Names the main nuclear contents.
rubric.how: Award up to 2 marks for correctly naming or describing nuclear contents, such as nucleoplasm, chromatin/chromosomes containing DNA, and the nucleolus.

rubric.why: States a key function of the nucleus.
rubric.description: Gives the function of the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the nucleus controls cell activities or contains hereditary information passed to daughter cells.

written.text: Write the uses of enzymes in different industries.
modelAnswer: In the food industry, enzymes are used in processes such as baking, cheese-making and brewing.
In the textile industry, enzymes are used to remove starch from cloth.
In the leather industry, enzymes are used to dehair hides.
In detergents, enzymes help remove protein and fat stains.
In the paper industry, enzymes are used in processing paper pulp.
Any five correct industry uses earn full credit.
written.followUp: Name five industries in which enzymes are used and give one use in each.

rubric.why: Awards credit for a correct food-industry application.
rubric.description: Food industry use, such as baking, cheese-making or brewing.
rubric.how: Name a food process in which enzymes are used.

rubric.why: Awards credit for a textile-industry application.
rubric.description: Textile industry use, such as removing starch from cloth.
rubric.how: State the textile process or purpose.

rubric.why: Awards credit for a leather-industry application.
rubric.description: Leather industry use, such as dehairing hides.
rubric.how: State a leather-processing use.

rubric.why: Awards credit for a detergent-industry application.
rubric.description: Detergents use enzymes to remove protein or fat stains.
rubric.how: Name a stain type that enzyme-containing detergents help remove.

rubric.why: Awards credit for another valid industrial use.
rubric.description: Paper industry use, such as processing pulp.
rubric.how: Name the industry and its enzyme-related process.

written.text: Describe the steps of light reaction of photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: Chlorophyll in the thylakoid membranes absorbs light energy and excites electrons.
Water undergoes photolysis, producing electrons, hydrogen ions and oxygen; oxygen is released.
The excited electrons pass through electron carriers, and their energy is used to form ATP by photophosphorylation.
Electrons and hydrogen reduce NADP to NADPH.
written.followUp: Explain how light energy is converted into ATP and NADPH during photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Establishes that light is absorbed by photosynthetic pigments.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy in the thylakoid membranes.
rubric.how: Identify the pigment or photosystem that absorbs light.

rubric.why: Recognises the splitting of water and its products.
rubric.description: Water is split, releasing oxygen, hydrogen ions and electrons.
rubric.how: State photolysis and at least one product.

rubric.why: Links electron movement to ATP formation.
rubric.description: Excited electrons pass along carriers; their energy is used to form ATP.
rubric.how: Mention electron transport and ATP formation.

rubric.why: Recognises the reducing power produced in the light reaction.
rubric.description: Electrons and hydrogen reduce NADP to NADPH.
rubric.how: Name NADPH or state that NADP is reduced.

written.text: Why is it called as Z-Scheme?
modelAnswer: In Photosystem II (P680), light excites electrons; electrons lost by PSII are replaced by electrons from the splitting of water.
The electrons pass through electron carriers to Photosystem I (P700), where light excites them again.
They are transferred to NADP, reducing it to NADPH.
When electron energy levels are plotted along this pathway, the rises and falls resemble the letter Z; therefore, it is called the Z-scheme.
written.followUp: Trace the movement of electrons in the Z-scheme from water to NADP.

rubric.why: Identifies the first photosystem in the electron pathway.
rubric.description: Light excites electrons in Photosystem II (P680); lost electrons are replaced by electrons from water.
rubric.how: Name PSII/P680 and connect its replacement electrons to water splitting.

rubric.why: Shows the pathway from PSII through carriers to PSI.
rubric.description: Electrons pass through an electron transport chain to Photosystem I (P700), where light excites them again.
rubric.how: Name the carriers and PSI, or state that electrons are excited again at PSI.

rubric.why: Explains the name and/or the final electron acceptor.
rubric.description: Electrons ultimately reduce NADP to NADPH; the energy-level path of the electrons resembles the letter Z, giving the scheme its name.
rubric.how: State the Z-shaped energy-level pattern or identify NADP as the final acceptor.

written.text: Describe the structure of stomach with labelled diagram. [Figure: labelled diagram requested]
modelAnswer: Draw a J-shaped outline about 8 cm high and 5 cm wide for the stomach.
Draw a 2 cm-long oesophagus entering its upper, cardiac end; label the fundus, body and pyloric region.
Draw a pyloric sphincter at the lower outlet and a 2 cm-long duodenum leading away from it; label both.
Draw folds inside the stomach and label them rugae; label gastric glands in the stomach wall.
The stomach is a muscular sac between the oesophagus and the small intestine; its inner lining has folds and gastric glands.
written.followUp: Draw and label a stomach, then describe its main regions and inner lining.

rubric.why: Checks the stomach’s entrance and its connection to the oesophagus.
rubric.description: Shows the oesophagus entering the stomach at its cardiac end.
rubric.how: Draw and label the oesophagus entering the upper end of the stomach.

rubric.why: Checks identification of the stomach’s regions.
rubric.description: Labels the fundus, body and pyloric region, or identifies the cardiac end.
rubric.how: Label the principal regions on the stomach diagram.

rubric.why: Checks the stomach’s outlet and its connection to the intestine.
rubric.description: Shows the pyloric outlet leading to the duodenum.
rubric.how: Label the pyloric sphincter or the duodenum at the lower outlet.

rubric.why: Checks a feature of the inner lining or stomach wall.
rubric.description: Shows the folded inner lining (rugae) or gastric glands.
rubric.how: Draw and label the folds or gastric glands.

written.text: Describe two scientific contributions of Bu-Ali Sina.
modelAnswer: Bu-Ali Sina was a renowned physician who wrote Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (The Canon of Medicine).
This influential work organised and advanced medical knowledge and was used as a medical reference for centuries.
written.followUp: Name one important medical book written by Bu-Ali Sina and state its importance.

rubric.why: Recognises Bu-Ali Sina's major medical writing.
rubric.description: He wrote Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb, known as The Canon of Medicine.
rubric.how: Name the book or give its accepted title.

rubric.why: Recognises his contribution to medicine.
rubric.description: His work systematised or advanced medical knowledge and was influential in the study of medicine.
rubric.how: State the medical significance of his work or his contribution as a physician.

written.text: What is meant by horticulture?
modelAnswer: Horticulture is the science and practice of cultivating plants.
It includes the cultivation of fruits, vegetables, flowers and ornamental plants.
written.followUp: What is floriculture, and how is it related to horticulture?

rubric.why: Identifies horticulture as the cultivation or growing of plants.
rubric.description: Horticulture is the science or practice of cultivating plants.
rubric.how: Give the central idea of plant cultivation.

rubric.why: Identifies examples of plants covered by horticulture.
rubric.description: It includes growing fruits, vegetables, flowers and ornamental plants.
rubric.how: Name at least one relevant plant group.

written.text: What is difference between theory and law?
modelAnswer: A scientific theory is a well-supported explanation of how or why a natural phenomenon occurs.
A scientific law describes a repeated pattern or relationship in nature; it states what happens, not why.
written.followUp: Explain one difference between a scientific hypothesis and a scientific theory.

rubric.why: Checks that a theory is understood as an explanatory account.
rubric.description: A theory explains how or why a natural phenomenon occurs.
rubric.how: State the explanatory role of a theory.

rubric.why: Checks that a law describes an observed regularity rather than explaining its cause.
rubric.description: A law describes a repeated natural pattern or relationship; it does not explain why it occurs.
rubric.how: State what a law describes and distinguish it from an explanation.

written.text: Differentiate between quantitative and qualitative observations.
modelAnswer: A quantitative observation is expressed numerically or by measurement, for example, the plant is 12 cm tall.
A qualitative observation describes a quality without numbers, for example, the flower is red.
written.followUp: Give one example each of a quantitative and a qualitative observation.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining feature of quantitative observations.
rubric.description: A quantitative observation uses numbers or measurements.
rubric.how: State that it is numerical or measured.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining feature of qualitative observations.
rubric.description: A qualitative observation describes a quality or characteristic without numerical measurement.
rubric.how: State that it is descriptive and non-numerical.

written.text: What is meant by species?
modelAnswer: A species is a group of similar organisms that can interbreed.
They produce fertile offspring.
written.followUp: Define genus.

rubric.why: Identifies the organisms grouped in a species and their ability to reproduce.
rubric.description: A species is a group of similar organisms capable of interbreeding.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a group of similar organisms that can interbreed.

rubric.why: Fertility of the offspring is a key part of the biological species definition.
rubric.description: They produce fertile offspring.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that interbreeding produces fertile offspring.

written.text: Define turgor pressure.
modelAnswer: Turgor pressure is the pressure exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall.
It develops when water enters the cell.
written.followUp: What is the role of turgor pressure in a plant cell?

rubric.why: Turgor pressure is the pressure exerted by the contents of a cell on its wall.
rubric.description: Defines turgor pressure as pressure exerted by cell contents against the cell wall.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the pressure and the cell contents or cytoplasm and cell wall involved.

rubric.why: Water entering the cell produces the pressure against the cell wall.
rubric.description: Links turgor pressure to water entering the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water enters or is taken up by the cell.

written.text: Differentiate between germline cells and somatic cells.
modelAnswer: Germline cells form gametes and pass genetic information to offspring.
Somatic cells are body cells other than germline cells.
written.followUp: Differentiate between asexual and sexual reproduction.

rubric.why: Germline cells give rise to gametes and carry hereditary information to offspring.
rubric.description: Identifies germline cells as cells that form gametes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that germline cells form gametes.

rubric.why: Somatic cells make up the body and are distinct from germline cells.
rubric.description: Identifies somatic cells as body cells other than germline cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing somatic cells as body cells distinct from germline cells.

written.text: What is meant by regeneration?
modelAnswer: Regeneration is the regrowth or replacement of a lost body part.
In some organisms, a body fragment can develop into a complete organism.
written.followUp: Name one organism that can reproduce by regeneration.

rubric.why: Regeneration involves regrowing or replacing a lost body part.
rubric.description: Regeneration is the regrowth or replacement of a lost body part.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning regrowth or replacement of a body part.

rubric.why: In some organisms, regeneration from a body fragment can produce a complete organism.
rubric.description: In some organisms, a body fragment can develop into a complete organism.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that a fragment may grow into a complete organism.

written.text: What is alcoholic fermentation?
modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose.
It produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
written.followUp: What are the products of lactic acid fermentation?

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation is an anaerobic process involving the breakdown of glucose.
rubric.description: Alcoholic fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that glucose is broken down without oxygen.

rubric.why: Ethanol and carbon dioxide are the characteristic products of alcoholic fermentation.
rubric.description: It produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both products.

written.text: Why light reactions are named as Z-scheme?
modelAnswer: The Z-scheme involves electron transfer through two photosystems, Photosystem II and Photosystem I.
The electron flow and energy level changes during transfer form a Z shape, so the pathway is called the Z-scheme.
written.followUp: Why is the electron transport pathway in cellular respiration called a respiratory chain?

rubric.why: The light-reaction electron pathway involves both photosystems.
rubric.description: Identifies the involvement of two photosystems.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both photosystems or stating that two photosystems are involved.

rubric.why: Changes in electron energy during transfer create a profile resembling the letter Z.
rubric.description: Explains that the electron-energy profile or electron flow forms a Z shape.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the electron flow or energy-level changes to a Z-shaped profile.

written.text: Write note on population and community levels.
modelAnswer: A population is a group of organisms of the same species living in a particular area at the same time.
A community consists of populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.
Population and community are levels of biological organization above the individual organism.
A community includes all the populations present in its area.
written.followUp: Explain the difference between an organism and a population.

rubric.why: A population consists of members of one species living in a particular area.
rubric.description: Defines a population level.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying organisms as the same species and 1 mark for stating that they live in the same area.

rubric.why: A community is made up of populations of different species that live and interact in an area.
rubric.description: Defines a community level.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying populations of different species and 1 mark for mentioning their shared area or interactions.

written.text: Describe endocytosis and exocytosis with the help of labelled diagram.
modelAnswer: Endocytosis is the uptake of material into a cell by the plasma membrane.
The plasma membrane folds inward around the material and pinches off to form a vesicle inside the cell.
Exocytosis is the release of material from a cell when an intracellular vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane.
The vesicle empties its contents outside the cell.
Diagram: draw and label the cell boundary as the plasma membrane and label the inside as cytoplasm.
For endocytosis, show the plasma membrane folding inward around material and forming an intracellular vesicle; add an inward arrow.
For exocytosis, show a vesicle inside the cell fusing with the plasma membrane and releasing material outside; add an outward arrow.
written.followUp: Describe the process by which a cell releases a substance using a vesicle.

rubric.why: Endocytosis brings material into the cell by forming a vesicle from the plasma membrane.
rubric.description: Describes endocytosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the membrane folding around or engulfing material and 1 mark for the resulting vesicle entering the cell.

rubric.why: Exocytosis releases material when an intracellular vesicle joins the plasma membrane.
rubric.description: Describes exocytosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane and 1 mark for release of contents outside the cell.

rubric.why: The labelled diagram should distinguish the inward movement of endocytosis from the outward release of exocytosis.
rubric.description: Provides a labelled diagram showing both processes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a clear diagram with the cell membrane, vesicle/material and correctly indicated directions.

written.text: Describe Lock and Key Model and Induced Fit Model in detail.
modelAnswer: In the lock and key model, an enzyme has a rigid active site with a particular shape.
Only a substrate with a complementary shape fits into the active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
In the induced fit model, the active site is flexible rather than completely rigid.
When the substrate binds, the active site changes shape to fit it more closely and catalyse the reaction.
written.followUp: Compare the lock and key and induced fit models of enzyme action.

rubric.why: The lock and key model explains enzyme specificity through a fixed active site that matches its substrate.
rubric.description: Explains the lock and key model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the active site has a fixed or specific shape and 1 mark for explaining that only a complementary substrate fits.

rubric.why: The induced fit model describes an active site that changes shape as the substrate binds.
rubric.description: Explains the induced fit model.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the active site is flexible or changes shape and 1 mark for explaining that substrate binding produces a better fit.

written.text: Define physiology and anatomy.
modelAnswer: Physiology is the study of the functions and processes of living organisms.
Anatomy is the study of the structure of living organisms and their parts.
written.followUp: Define morphology and explain what it studies.

rubric.why: Physiology is concerned with the functions and processes of living organisms.
rubric.description: Defines physiology.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that physiology studies the functions or functioning of organisms.

rubric.why: Anatomy is concerned with the structure of organisms and their parts.
rubric.description: Defines anatomy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that anatomy studies the structure of organisms.

written.text: Define population and community.
modelAnswer: A population is a group of organisms of the same species living in a particular area.
A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area.
written.followUp: What is a population? Give one example of a population in an ecosystem.

rubric.why: A population is made up of organisms belonging to the same species in a defined area.
rubric.description: Defines population.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including organisms of the same species living in the same area.

rubric.why: A community includes populations of different species living and interacting in a shared area.
rubric.description: Defines community.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including populations of different species in a shared area or their interactions.

written.text: Define deforestation and write its causes.
modelAnswer: Deforestation is the removal or clearing of forests, usually by cutting down trees.
Its causes include clearing land for agriculture, obtaining timber or fuel, urbanization, road construction and forest fires.
written.followUp: State two effects of deforestation on the environment.

rubric.why: Deforestation means the removal or clearing of forest cover.
rubric.description: Defines deforestation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the clearing or removal of forests or trees.

rubric.why: Common causes include clearing land for farming, obtaining timber or fuel, urban development, road construction and fires.
rubric.description: States causes of deforestation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving one valid cause.

written.text: Write any two characteristics of organisms of kingdom monera.
modelAnswer: Organisms of kingdom Monera are unicellular.
They are prokaryotic and lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
written.followUp: What is the main difference between organisms of kingdom Monera and those of kingdom Protista?

rubric.why: Monerans are unicellular organisms.
rubric.description: Gives one characteristic of Monera.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Monerans are unicellular.

rubric.why: Monerans are prokaryotic and lack a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
rubric.description: Gives another characteristic of Monera.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Monerans are prokaryotic or lack a membrane-bound nucleus or organelles.

written.text: Define hypotonic and hypertonic solutions.
modelAnswer: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the solution with which it is compared.
A hypertonic solution has a higher solute concentration than the solution with which it is compared.
written.followUp: Define isotonic and hypertonic solutions.

rubric.why: A hypotonic solution has a lower solute concentration than the solution it is compared with.

written.text: What is the difference between Diffusion and Osmosis?
modelAnswer: Diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration.
Osmosis is the movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution.
written.followUp: Differentiate between diffusion and osmosis.

rubric.why: Diffusion is the net movement of particles down their concentration gradient.
rubric.description: Defines diffusion as movement of particles from higher to lower concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the direction of movement and the term particles or molecules.

rubric.why: Osmosis specifically involves water moving across a selectively permeable membrane.
rubric.description: Distinguishes osmosis as movement of water through a selectively permeable membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water and the membrane.

written.text: Differentiate between Endocytosis and Exocytosis.
modelAnswer: Endocytosis is the uptake of material into a cell when the cell membrane engulfs it and forms a vesicle.
Exocytosis is the release of material from a cell when a vesicle fuses with the cell membrane.
written.followUp: Explain how materials enter a cell by endocytosis and leave it by exocytosis.

rubric.why: Endocytosis brings material into the cell by enclosing it in a membrane-bound vesicle.
rubric.description: Explains that endocytosis takes material into the cell in a vesicle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for inward movement and vesicle formation or membrane engulfment.

rubric.why: Exocytosis releases material when a vesicle fuses with the cell membrane.
rubric.description: Explains that exocytosis releases material from the cell by vesicle fusion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for outward release and vesicle fusion or equivalent.

written.text: Define Cell Cycle and write its major phases.
modelAnswer: The cell cycle is the sequence of events from one cell division to the next.
Its major phases are interphase and the mitotic phase (M phase).
written.followUp: Name the two major phases of the cell cycle and state what happens in each.

rubric.why: The cell cycle is the sequence of events from one cell division to the next.
rubric.description: Defines the cell cycle as the sequence of events between successive cell divisions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition that describes the events from one division to the next.

rubric.why: Interphase and the mitotic phase are the major phases of the cell cycle.
rubric.description: Names interphase and the mitotic phase (M phase).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both major phases.

written.text: What is meant by Phagoplasm? Write its role in plant's cell division.
modelAnswer: “Phagoplasm” in this question appears to refer to the phragmoplast, a structure of microtubules formed during plant-cell division.
It guides the formation of the cell plate between the daughter nuclei; the cell plate develops into a new cell wall separating the daughter cells.
written.followUp: What is a phragmoplast, and how does it help in cytokinesis in plant cells?

rubric.why: The term in the question appears to refer to the phragmoplast, a microtubule structure involved in plant-cell cytokinesis.
rubric.description: Identifies the phagoplasm/phragmoplast as a structure associated with plant-cell division, particularly the cell plate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the structure as the phragmoplast or associating it with microtubules and the cell plate.

rubric.why: The phragmoplast helps organize cell-plate formation between the daughter nuclei.
rubric.description: States that it helps form or guide the cell plate, which separates the daughter cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the role in cell-plate formation or separation of the daughter cells.

written.text: What is the difference between Benign and Malignant tumors?
modelAnswer: Benign tumors are non-cancerous, usually remain localized, and do not spread to other parts of the body.
Malignant tumors are cancerous; they invade surrounding tissues and may spread to other parts of the body (metastasis).
written.followUp: Differentiate between benign and malignant tumors.

rubric.why: Benign tumors are non-cancerous, usually remain localized, and do not spread to other parts of the body.
rubric.description: States that benign tumors are non-cancerous and remain localized without spreading.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the non-spreading, localized nature of benign tumors.

rubric.why: Malignant tumors are cancerous, invade surrounding tissues, and may spread to other parts of the body by metastasis.
rubric.description: States that malignant tumors are cancerous and invade or spread.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing invasion into surrounding tissues or spread to other parts of the body.

written.text: What is the difference between Catabolism and Anabolism?
modelAnswer: Catabolism is the breakdown of complex molecules into simpler molecules, releasing energy.
Anabolism is the synthesis of complex molecules from simpler molecules, requiring energy.
written.followUp: Differentiate between anabolic and catabolic reactions, including their energy changes.

rubric.why: Catabolism breaks complex molecules into simpler molecules and releases energy.
rubric.description: Defines catabolism as the breakdown of complex molecules into simpler ones.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the breakdown direction of catabolism.

rubric.why: Anabolism synthesizes complex molecules from simpler molecules and requires energy.
rubric.description: Defines anabolism as the synthesis of complex molecules from simpler ones.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the synthesis direction of anabolism.

written.text: What is meant by Alcoholic fermentation and Lactic acid fermentation?
modelAnswer: Alcoholic fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose by yeast to form ethanol and carbon dioxide.
Lactic acid fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose to form lactic acid, for example in muscle cells or some bacteria.
written.followUp: State the products of alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.

rubric.why: Alcoholic fermentation converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide, usually through yeast action in the absence of oxygen.
rubric.description: Defines alcoholic fermentation and identifies its products.
rubric.how: Award for the anaerobic conversion to ethanol and carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: Lactic acid fermentation converts glucose into lactic acid without oxygen.
rubric.description: Defines lactic acid fermentation and identifies its product.
rubric.how: Award for the conversion to lactic acid, typically in muscles or bacteria.

written.text: Define Bio-energetics.
modelAnswer: Bio-energetics is the study of energy relationships and energy transformations in living organisms.
written.followUp: What does bio-energetics study?

rubric.why: Bio-energetics concerns energy in living systems.
rubric.description: Defines bio-energetics as the study of energy relations or transformations in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award for linking the study of energy to living organisms.

written.text: What is the difference between Saturated and Unsaturated fatty acid? Give one example of each.
modelAnswer: A saturated fatty acid has no carbon-carbon double bonds; an unsaturated fatty acid has one or more carbon-carbon double bonds.
Palmitic acid is an example of a saturated fatty acid, while oleic acid is an example of an unsaturated fatty acid.
written.followUp: Distinguish between saturated and unsaturated fatty acids and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Saturated fatty acids have no carbon-carbon double bonds; unsaturated fatty acids have one or more.
rubric.description: Distinguishes the two types by the presence or absence of carbon-carbon double bonds.
rubric.how: Award for a correct contrast between saturated and unsaturated fatty acids.

rubric.why: Palmitic or stearic acid is saturated; oleic or linoleic acid is unsaturated.
rubric.description: Gives an appropriate example of each type.
rubric.how: Award when examples correctly represent both categories.

written.text: What is meant by Macronutrients? Give two examples.
modelAnswer: Macronutrients are nutrients required by organisms, especially plants, in relatively large amounts.
Examples of plant macronutrients include nitrogen and phosphorus.
written.followUp: Define macronutrients and name two examples needed by plants.

rubric.why: Macronutrients are nutrients required in relatively large amounts.
rubric.description: Defines macronutrients by the large quantity required.
rubric.how: Award for stating that they are needed in large amounts.

rubric.why: Examples of plant macronutrients include nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
rubric.description: Names two valid examples of macronutrients.
rubric.how: Award for any two correct examples.

written.text: Explain any four careers related to Biology.
modelAnswer: Agriculture: biologists help improve crops and develop better farming practices.
Animal husbandry: biological knowledge is used to breed, feed and care for livestock.
Fisheries: biologists help breed fish and manage fish production and aquatic resources.
Forestry: knowledge of biology is used to manage forests and protect trees and wildlife.
written.followUp: Explain four other careers related to Biology, apart from medicine.

rubric.why: Biological knowledge is used to improve crops and farming practices.
rubric.description: Explains agriculture as a biology-related career.
rubric.how: Award for linking biology with crop production or farming.

rubric.why: Biology supports the breeding, care and management of animals.
rubric.description: Explains animal husbandry or veterinary work as a biology-related career.
rubric.how: Award for a career explanation involving animal health, care or breeding.

rubric.why: Biology is used in fish breeding, production and fisheries management.
rubric.description: Explains fisheries or aquaculture as a biology-related career.
rubric.how: Award for linking the career with fish or aquatic organisms.

rubric.why: Forestry applies biology to forests and trees; other biological careers include biotechnology and environmental biology.
rubric.description: Explains one further biology-related career.
rubric.how: Award for a relevant career and its biological application.

written.text: Define Photosynthesis and describe the role of light and chlorophyll on photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy.
Oxygen is released during this process.
Light provides the energy needed for photosynthesis.
Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts traps light energy for the process.
written.followUp: Define transpiration and describe the role of stomata in this process.

rubric.why: Defines photosynthesis as the process by which plants make food.
rubric.description: Definition of photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for stating that green plants make food (or glucose) from carbon dioxide and water using light energy; award 1 mark for a partly correct definition.

rubric.why: Identifies light as the energy source for photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Role of light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that light provides energy for photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Explains that chlorophyll captures light energy.
rubric.description: Role of chlorophyll.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for explaining that chlorophyll traps or absorbs light energy; award 1 mark if chlorophyll is named but its role is unclear.

written.text: What is meant by Vegetative Organs? Write two examples of Vegetative Organs.
modelAnswer: Vegetative organs are the non-reproductive parts of a plant that perform functions such as absorption, support and food-making.
The vegetative organs are roots, stems and leaves.
Two examples are the root and the stem.
written.followUp: What are reproductive organs? Give two examples.

rubric.why: Identifies the main vegetative organs of a plant.
rubric.description: Names the vegetative organs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming roots, stems and leaves as the vegetative organs.

rubric.why: Provides two examples of vegetative organs.
rubric.description: Two examples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for giving any two correct examples, such as root and stem.

written.text: Write any two observations of "A.F.A King".
modelAnswer: A. F. A. King observed that malaria was common in marshy places where mosquitoes were abundant.
He also observed that people sleeping outdoors or without mosquito protection were more likely to get malaria.
written.followUp: Give two observations that led scientists to investigate the spread of malaria.

rubric.why: Includes the observed association between malaria and mosquitoes or marshy areas.
rubric.description: First observation of A. F. A. King.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that malaria was common in places where mosquitoes were abundant, particularly marshy areas.

rubric.why: Includes an observation relating people's exposure to mosquitoes and malaria.
rubric.description: Second observation of A. F. A. King.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that people sleeping outdoors or without mosquito protection were more likely to get malaria, or that mosquito nets offered protection.

written.text: Differentiate between Prions and Viroids.
modelAnswer: Prions are infectious protein particles and do not contain nucleic acid.
Viroids are small infectious RNA molecules without a protein coat; they mainly infect plants.
written.followUp: Differentiate between bacteria and viruses.

rubric.why: Identifies the composition of prions.
rubric.description: Prions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that prions are infectious protein particles and lack nucleic acid.

rubric.why: Identifies the composition or host of viroids.
rubric.description: Viroids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that viroids are small infectious RNA molecules without a protein coat, commonly infecting plants.

written.text: Describe the aims of Classification.
modelAnswer: Classification organizes the great diversity of organisms into groups, making them easier to study.
It helps in identifying organisms and understanding their similarities, differences and relationships.
written.followUp: State two reasons why organisms are grouped into kingdoms.

rubric.why: Recognizes that classification organizes the diversity of organisms.
rubric.description: Organization of organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that classification arranges organisms into groups and makes their diversity easier to study.

rubric.why: Gives another purpose of classification.
rubric.description: Identification or comparison of organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that classification helps identify organisms, compare similarities and differences, or show relationships among them.

written.text: What is meant by Endocytosis? Also write names its types.
modelAnswer: Endocytosis is the process by which a cell takes in material as its plasma membrane folds inward and forms a vesicle.
Its two types are phagocytosis and pinocytosis.
written.followUp: Define exocytosis and state what happens to a vesicle during this process.

rubric.why: Defines the movement of material into a cell by endocytosis.
rubric.description: Definition of endocytosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the cell takes in material by the plasma membrane folding inward and forming a vesicle.

rubric.why: Names both types of endocytosis.
rubric.description: Types of endocytosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming phagocytosis and pinocytosis.

written.text: Define Cell Cycle and write the names of its phases.
modelAnswer: The cell cycle is the sequence of events that a cell undergoes from its formation until it divides.
Its two main phases are interphase and the mitotic phase (M phase).
written.followUp: Define mitosis and name its main stages.

rubric.why: Defines the cell cycle as the events a cell undergoes from its formation until it divides.
rubric.description: Definition of the cell cycle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the cell cycle as the sequence of events from a cell's formation until its division.

rubric.why: Names the two main phases of the cell cycle.
rubric.description: Phases of the cell cycle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming interphase and the mitotic phase (M phase).

written.text: When and who discovered crossing over in Drosophila Melanogaster?
modelAnswer: Crossing over in Drosophila melanogaster was discovered by Thomas Hunt Morgan in 1911.
written.followUp: Who first observed crossing over, and in which organism and year?

rubric.why: Identifies when crossing over was discovered.
rubric.description: Gives the year 1911.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct year.

rubric.why: Identifies the scientist who discovered crossing over in Drosophila.
rubric.description: Names Thomas Hunt Morgan.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct scientist.

written.text: Define Mitosis and Mitotic Spindle.
modelAnswer: Mitosis is the division of a cell nucleus into two daughter nuclei, each with the same number of chromosomes as the parent nucleus.
written.followUp: Define crossing over and name the scientist who first observed it.

rubric.why: A definition of mitosis must identify it as nuclear division.
rubric.description: Defines mitosis as division of the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying nuclear division.

rubric.why: Mitosis produces two nuclei with the same chromosome number as the parent nucleus.
rubric.description: States that mitosis forms two daughter nuclei with the same chromosome number.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this outcome.

written.text: Describe briefly “Lock and Key” model of Enzymes. Who proposed it?
modelAnswer: In the lock-and-key model, a substrate with a shape complementary to an enzyme’s active site fits into it, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
The model was proposed by Emil Fischer.
written.followUp: Define a chromosome and state one function of the mitotic spindle.

rubric.why: The model explains enzyme action through the fit between the substrate and the enzyme's active site.
rubric.description: Explains that a substrate with a complementary shape fits the enzyme's active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complementary fit or formation of an enzyme-substrate complex.

rubric.why: Emil Fischer proposed the lock-and-key model.
rubric.description: Names Emil Fischer as the proposer.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct name.

written.text: Define two types of energy in living organisms.
modelAnswer: Kinetic energy is the energy of motion, such as the movement of an organism or its parts.
Potential energy is stored energy due to an object's position or structure.
written.followUp: What is chemical energy, and how is it stored in living organisms?

rubric.why: Kinetic energy is one of the two main forms of energy in living organisms.
rubric.description: Defines kinetic energy as energy of motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct form and definition.

rubric.why: Potential energy is energy stored due to position or structure.
rubric.description: Defines potential energy as stored energy due to position or structure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct form and definition.

written.text: Write the effect of Carbondioxide concentration on Photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: As carbon dioxide concentration increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases while carbon dioxide is a limiting factor.
The rate eventually levels off when another factor limits photosynthesis.
written.followUp: What happens to the rate of photosynthesis as light intensity increases?

rubric.why: Increasing carbon dioxide concentration raises the rate of photosynthesis when carbon dioxide is limiting.
rubric.description: States that increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the positive effect of increased carbon dioxide.

rubric.why: The increase does not continue indefinitely; another limiting factor eventually restricts the rate.
rubric.description: States that the rate levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the limit or plateau.

written.text: Give any two reasons for creation of transpirational pull.
modelAnswer: Evaporation of water from the leaf cells during transpiration creates tension in the xylem.
Cohesion between water molecules helps transmit this pull along the continuous water column.
written.followUp: State two factors that increase the rate of transpiration.

rubric.why: Evaporation of water from leaf cells creates tension or suction in the xylem.
rubric.description: Gives water evaporation or loss from the leaves as a cause of transpirational pull.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying evaporation or water loss from leaves.

rubric.why: Cohesion between water molecules, and adhesion to xylem walls, helps transmit the pull through the water column.
rubric.description: Gives cohesion between water molecules or adhesion to xylem walls as a cause.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either property.

written.text: Write two effects of temperature on the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: A rise in temperature increases evaporation from leaf surfaces, so the rate of transpiration increases.
A fall in temperature reduces evaporation, so the rate of transpiration decreases.
written.followUp: How does wind affect the rate of transpiration?

rubric.why: A rise in temperature increases evaporation from leaf surfaces and thus increases transpiration.
rubric.description: States that higher temperature increases the rate of transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of rising temperature.

rubric.why: A fall in temperature reduces evaporation and lowers the rate of transpiration.
rubric.description: States that lower temperature decreases the rate of transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of falling temperature.

written.text: Write difference between Prokaryotic and Eukaryotic cells.
modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a membrane bound nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane bound organelles; eukaryotic cells contain membrane bound organelles.
Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller and have 70S ribosomes; eukaryotic cells are generally larger and have 80S ribosomes.
Prokaryotic DNA is usually circular and lies in the nucleoid; eukaryotic DNA is organized into linear chromosomes in the nucleus.
written.followUp: State four differences between an organ and an organ system.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus, while eukaryotic cells have one.
rubric.description: Compares the nucleus in the two cell types.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for correctly contrasting both cell types; award 1 mark for a correct statement about only one type.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles, whereas eukaryotic cells contain them.
rubric.description: Compares membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller and have 70S ribosomes; eukaryotic cells are generally larger and have 80S ribosomes.
rubric.description: Gives another valid structural difference.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct comparison, such as size or ribosomes.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic DNA is usually circular and lies in the nucleoid; eukaryotic DNA is organized into linear chromosomes in the nucleus.
rubric.description: Compares the genetic material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct contrast in DNA or chromosome organization.

written.text: Write any four characteristics of Enzyme.
modelAnswer: Enzymes are biological catalysts that speed up biochemical reactions.
They are not consumed in the reactions and can be reused.
Each enzyme is specific to a particular substrate or reaction.
Enzymes are proteins and work best at an optimum temperature and pH.
written.followUp: Write any four characteristics of viruses.

rubric.why: Enzymes are biological catalysts that increase the rate of biochemical reactions.
rubric.description: Identifies enzymes as biological catalysts that speed up reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying enzymes as biological catalysts or stating that they speed up reactions.

rubric.why: Enzymes are not used up in reactions and can be used again.
rubric.description: States that enzymes remain unchanged or can be reused.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this characteristic.

rubric.why: Each enzyme acts on a particular substrate or reaction.
rubric.description: States that enzymes are specific.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for enzyme specificity.

rubric.why: Enzymes are proteins and have optimum conditions for their activity.
rubric.description: Gives another characteristic of enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that enzymes are proteins or that they have an optimum temperature or pH.

written.text: What is Biogeography?
modelAnswer: Biogeography is the study of the geographical distribution of organisms, both living and extinct.
written.followUp: Define taxonomy and state what it helps biologists do.

rubric.why: Biogeography is the study of the geographical distribution of organisms.
rubric.description: Defines biogeography.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for identifying the study of organisms' geographical distribution; 1 mark for a partial definition.

written.text: What are deductions?
modelAnswer: Deductions are logical conclusions drawn from observations, often using prior knowledge.
written.followUp: What is a hypothesis?

rubric.why: Deductions are logical conclusions or inferences drawn from observations, often using prior knowledge.
rubric.description: Defines deductions.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for defining deductions as conclusions or inferences drawn from observations; award 1 mark for mentioning a conclusion or inference without linking it to observations.

written.text: Write the scientific name of onion and pea?
modelAnswer: Onion: Allium cepa.
Pea: Pisum sativum.
written.followUp: Write the scientific names of mango and wheat.

rubric.why: Allium cepa is the scientific name of onion.
rubric.description: Gives the scientific name of onion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct binomial name.

rubric.why: Pisum sativum is the scientific name of pea.
rubric.description: Gives the scientific name of pea.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct binomial name.

written.text: State the principles of binomial nomenclature.
modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature gives each organism a two-word scientific name: the genus name followed by the species name.
The genus name begins with a capital letter, while the species name begins with a lowercase letter; the names are written in italics or underlined separately when handwritten.
written.followUp: State the rules for writing the scientific name of an organism.

rubric.why: A binomial name has two parts: the genus name and the species name.
rubric.description: Identifies the two parts of a binomial name.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both genus and species.

rubric.why: Scientific names follow conventions for capitalization and formatting.
rubric.description: States a convention for writing scientific names.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the capitalization convention or the italics/underlining convention.

written.text: What is meant by collenchyma tissue?
modelAnswer: Collenchyma is a simple permanent tissue made of living, elongated cells with walls unevenly thickened at the corners.
It provides support and flexibility to young parts of the plant, such as stems and leaves.
written.followUp: What is the function of sclerenchyma tissue?

rubric.why: Collenchyma consists of living cells whose walls are unevenly thickened at the corners.
rubric.description: Describes the cells and their characteristic wall thickening.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying living cells and uneven thickening at the corners.

rubric.why: Collenchyma supports young plant parts while allowing them to bend without breaking.
rubric.description: States the tissue’s role in young plant parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for support and flexibility in young parts.

written.text: What are biocatalysts?
modelAnswer: Biocatalysts are biological catalysts, usually enzymes, that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms.
They are not used up or permanently changed in the reactions they catalyse.
written.followUp: What are enzymes, and how do they affect chemical reactions in living organisms?

rubric.why: Biocatalysts are biological catalysts, usually enzymes.
rubric.description: Defines biocatalysts as biological catalysts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as biological catalysts or enzymes that act as catalysts.

rubric.why: Biocatalysts speed up chemical reactions and are not used up in the reactions they catalyse.
rubric.description: States their effect on reactions and that they are not consumed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they speed up reactions and are not used up.

written.text: What is meant by active site of an enzyme?
modelAnswer: The active site is the specific region of an enzyme to which its substrate binds.
The enzyme-catalysed reaction takes place at this site.
written.followUp: How does a substrate bind to an enzyme?

rubric.why: The active site is the particular region of an enzyme to which its substrate binds.
rubric.description: Defines the active site as the enzyme region where the substrate binds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for locating substrate binding on a specific enzyme region.

rubric.why: The enzyme-catalysed reaction takes place at the active site.
rubric.description: States that catalysis occurs at the active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the role of the active site in the reaction.

written.text: What is the role of ATP in the function of cell?
modelAnswer: ATP stores energy in the bonds between its phosphate groups.
When energy is needed, ATP releases it for cellular activities; therefore, ATP acts as the cell’s energy currency.
written.followUp: Why is ATP called the energy currency of the cell?

rubric.why: ATP stores energy in the bonds between its phosphate groups.
rubric.description: States where ATP stores energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking stored energy with ATP’s phosphate bonds or groups.

rubric.why: ATP releases energy that cells use to carry out their activities.
rubric.description: Explains how ATP provides energy to the cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that ATP supplies or releases energy for cellular activities.

written.text: Define lactic acid fermentation.
modelAnswer: Lactic acid fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose to form lactic acid.
It releases only a small amount of energy.
written.followUp: Define alcoholic fermentation.

rubric.why: Lactic acid fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose to form lactic acid.
rubric.description: Identifies the anaerobic conversion of glucose into lactic acid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the absence of oxygen and the product, lactic acid.

rubric.why: This process releases only a small amount of energy.
rubric.description: Mentions the small energy yield.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that little energy is released.

written.text: Write the role of potassium in plant life?
modelAnswer: Potassium activates several enzymes in plants.
It also helps regulate the opening and closing of stomata.
written.followUp: State one role of magnesium in plant life.

rubric.why: Potassium activates several enzymes in plants.
rubric.description: States potassium’s role in enzyme activation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that potassium activates enzymes.

rubric.why: Potassium helps regulate the opening and closing of stomata.
rubric.description: States potassium’s role in stomatal regulation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking potassium with regulation of stomata.

written.text: Define organic fertilizer and give an example.
modelAnswer: An organic fertilizer is a natural material made from plant or animal matter and added to soil to improve its fertility.
Farmyard manure is an example.
written.followUp: What is compost, and how does it improve soil?

rubric.why: Organic fertilizer is a natural material from plant or animal matter that is added to soil to improve fertility.
rubric.description: Defines organic fertilizer by its source and purpose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing its plant or animal origin and its use as a fertilizer to improve soil.

rubric.why: Farmyard manure and compost are examples of organic fertilizers.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

written.text: What is difference between pepsin and pepsinogen?
modelAnswer: Pepsin is the active protein-digesting enzyme in the stomach.
Pepsinogen is its inactive precursor; hydrochloric acid activates it to form pepsin.
written.followUp: Differentiate between trypsin and trypsinogen.

rubric.why: Distinguishes pepsin as the active enzyme.
rubric.description: Pepsin is the active form of the enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying pepsin as active.

rubric.why: Distinguishes pepsinogen as the inactive form that becomes pepsin.
rubric.description: Pepsinogen is an inactive precursor that is activated by hydrochloric acid in the stomach.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying pepsinogen as inactive or as the precursor of pepsin.

written.text: Write four sources to get protein.
modelAnswer: Four sources of protein are meat, fish, eggs and pulses.
written.followUp: Name four sources of carbohydrates.

rubric.why: Credits two valid protein sources.
rubric.description: Any two suitable sources of protein, such as meat, fish, eggs, milk, pulses, beans or nuts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each pair of valid sources; do not award twice for the same source.

written.text: Define any five divisions of Biology.
modelAnswer: Morphology is the study of the external form and structure of organisms.

Physiology is the study of the functions of organisms and their parts.

Ecology is the study of the relationships of organisms with one another and with their environment.

written.text: Explain the structure of cell membrane.
modelAnswer: The cell membrane is a thin, flexible phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it.
The hydrophilic heads of the phospholipids face outward toward the watery environments on both sides of the membrane.
The hydrophobic tails face inward toward one another.
This arrangement is described by the fluid mosaic model, and the membrane is selectively permeable.

written.text: Describe the factors which affect the rate of enzyme action.
modelAnswer: Temperature: enzyme activity rises as temperature increases up to the enzyme's optimum; above this, the enzyme may denature and its activity falls.
pH: each enzyme works best at an optimum pH; a pH that is too high or too low changes the active site and reduces activity.
Substrate concentration: increasing substrate concentration raises the reaction rate until the enzyme's active sites are saturated.
Enzyme concentration: increasing the amount of enzyme raises the reaction rate if enough substrate is available.
Inhibitors: inhibitors reduce enzyme activity by interfering with the enzyme or blocking its active site.
written.followUp: Explain how temperature and pH affect enzyme activity.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of temperature on enzyme activity.
rubric.description: Enzyme activity increases with temperature up to an optimum; higher temperatures can denature the enzyme and reduce activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing an optimum or heat denaturation and its effect on activity.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of pH on enzyme activity.
rubric.description: Each enzyme has an optimum pH; values above or below it alter the active site and lower activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an optimum pH or explaining that unsuitable pH lowers activity.

rubric.why: Explains how substrate availability affects the reaction rate.
rubric.description: Increasing substrate concentration increases the rate until the enzyme's active sites are saturated.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the increase in rate or the saturation limit.

rubric.why: Explains the effect of enzyme amount on reaction rate.
rubric.description: Increasing enzyme concentration increases the reaction rate when sufficient substrate is available.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking more enzyme or active sites to a higher rate.

rubric.why: Credits the effect of inhibitors on enzyme action.
rubric.description: Inhibitors reduce enzyme activity, for example by blocking an active site or interfering with the enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that inhibitors lower enzyme activity or explaining how they do so.

modelAnswer: Skeletal (striated) muscle has long fibres, is usually attached to bones and works voluntarily.
Smooth (unstriated) muscle has spindle-shaped cells, occurs in the walls of internal organs and works involuntarily.

written.text: What are light reactions and Dark reactions. Write the summary of the events of Dark reactions in Photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: Light reactions occur in the thylakoid membranes (grana) and require light; they produce ATP and NADPH and release oxygen from the splitting of water.
Dark reactions (the Calvin cycle) occur in the stroma. They do not require light directly and use ATP and NADPH to fix carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP, forming an unstable six-carbon compound that splits into two molecules of PGA.
ATP and NADPH reduce PGA to PGAL (G3P).
Some PGAL is used to form sugars, while the rest regenerates RuBP.

written.text: Explain five types of epithelial tissues.
modelAnswer: Squamous epithelium has thin, flat cells and forms linings, such as the lining of the mouth or blood vessels.
Cuboidal epithelium has cube-shaped cells and is found in kidney tubules and glands, where it performs absorption or secretion.
Columnar epithelium has tall, pillar-like cells and lines parts of the digestive tract, where it helps in absorption and secretion.
Ciliated epithelium has cilia on its free surface; the cilia move material, such as mucus in the respiratory tract.
Glandular epithelium is specialized for secretion and forms glands that release substances such as enzymes or hormones.
written.followUp: Describe the structure and function of connective tissue and muscular tissue.

rubric.why: Identifies a correct epithelial type and its characteristic structure or location.
rubric.description: Squamous epithelium consists of thin, flat cells and forms a lining.
rubric.how: Award for correctly describing squamous epithelium and its thin, flat cells or lining role.

rubric.why: Identifies cuboidal epithelium and a characteristic location or function.
rubric.description: Cuboidal epithelium has cube-shaped cells and is found in glands or kidney tubules, where it may secrete or absorb substances.
rubric.how: Award for correctly describing cuboidal epithelium and a characteristic location or function.

rubric.why: Identifies columnar epithelium and its characteristic location or function.
rubric.description: Columnar epithelium has tall cells and lines parts of the digestive tract, where it helps in absorption and secretion.
rubric.how: Award for correctly describing columnar epithelium and its tall cells, location or function.

rubric.why: Covers the remaining epithelial types and their characteristic function.
rubric.description: Ciliated epithelium moves material using cilia; glandular epithelium is specialized for secretion.
rubric.how: Award for correctly describing both ciliated and glandular epithelium, including the function of either type.

written.text: Define ATP. Discuss its composition by drawing its structure.
modelAnswer: ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is the cell’s energy-carrying molecule, often called its energy currency.
Adenine joined to ribose forms adenosine.
Adenosine is joined to three phosphate groups to form ATP.
Structure:  Adenine — Ribose — P ~ P ~ P  (P = phosphate group; three phosphate groups)

rubric.description: Adenine combined with ribose forms adenosine.
rubric.how: Look for adenine, ribose, and their combination as adenosine.

rubric.description: Adenosine is joined to three phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Look for three phosphate groups or the term triphosphate.

rubric.why: Award for a correct labelled structural representation showing adenosine and three phosphates.

written.text: Discuss cardiovascular disorders.
modelAnswer: Atherosclerosis is the build-up of fatty deposits (plaques) in the walls of arteries.
These deposits narrow the arteries and reduce blood flow.
Hypertension is persistently high blood pressure.
If a coronary artery is blocked, the heart muscle may lose its blood supply and a heart attack may occur.

written.text: Describe the importance of fertilizers.
modelAnswer: Fertilizers supply plants with essential mineral nutrients.
They provide important nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium.
They replenish nutrients in the soil and help maintain soil fertility.
They promote healthy growth and development of plants.
They can increase crop yield and food production.

modelAnswer: Organisms of kingdom Monera are unicellular and prokaryotic.

written.text: Write down two principles of binomial nomenclature.

written.text: What is active transport?
modelAnswer: Active transport is the movement of substances across a cell membrane against their concentration gradient.
It requires energy, usually supplied by ATP.

written.text: Differentiate between primary & secondary cell wall.
modelAnswer: The primary cell wall forms first, while the cell is growing, and is usually thin and flexible.
The secondary cell wall is deposited inside the primary wall after cell growth and is usually thicker.

written.text: What is meant by cell cycle? Write the name of its two phases.
modelAnswer: The cell cycle is the sequence of events a cell undergoes from one cell division to the next.
Its two main phases are interphase and the mitotic phase (M phase).

rubric.why: Interphase is one of the two main stages of the cell cycle.

written.text: What is difference between karyokinesis and cytokinesis?

written.text: What is effect of light intensity and temperature on the rate of photosynthesis?
modelAnswer: As light intensity increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases until it reaches a saturation point.
As temperature rises, the rate increases up to an optimum; above the optimum, the rate falls because photosynthetic enzymes are affected.

written.text: Write components of human food.

written.text: Describe the role of iron in plant's life.
modelAnswer: Iron is required for the formation of chlorophyll, although it is not a constituent of the chlorophyll molecule.

written.text: Write the factors which affect the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: The rate of transpiration is affected by light intensity, temperature, humidity and wind or air movement.

written.text: Describe any five differences between prokaryotic cells and eukaryotic cells.
modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells have no true nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane.
Prokaryotic DNA is generally circular; eukaryotic chromosomes are linear.
Prokaryotic cells have 70S ribosomes; eukaryotic cells have 80S ribosomes in their cytoplasm.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane bound organelles; eukaryotic cells have them, for example mitochondria.
Prokaryotic cells divide by binary fission; eukaryotic cells divide by mitosis or meiosis.

rubric.description: Compares ribosomes.
rubric.how: Award for stating that prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes and eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes in their cytoplasm.

written.text: Explain Active Transport.
modelAnswer: Active transport is the movement of substances across a cell membrane against their concentration gradient, from a lower concentration to a higher concentration.
It requires energy, usually supplied as ATP during respiration.
Carrier or transport proteins in the cell membrane assist in moving the substances.
For example, root hair cells use active transport to absorb mineral ions from the soil, even when their concentration is lower in the soil than in the cells.
Active transport is selective and also helps cells absorb substances such as glucose and amino acids.

written.text: Write characteristics of Five Kingdoms.
modelAnswer: Monera: Organisms are unicellular and prokaryotic; their cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus.
Protista: Organisms are eukaryotic and mostly unicellular; they may be autotrophic or heterotrophic.
Fungi: Organisms are eukaryotic and mostly multicellular, have cell walls, and obtain food heterotrophically by absorption.
Plantae: Organisms are multicellular eukaryotes with cell walls; they are autotrophic and make food by photosynthesis.
Animalia: Organisms are multicellular eukaryotes without cell walls; they are heterotrophic and usually capable of movement.
