written.text: Write the structure of Human Heart with Diagram.
modelAnswer: The heart is a hollow, muscular organ enclosed by a protective covering; it has four chambers: right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium and left ventricle.
The septum separates the right and left sides of the heart; valves between the chambers and at the exits of the ventricles prevent backflow.
The venae cavae bring deoxygenated blood from the body to the right atrium; it passes through the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle and leaves through the pulmonary artery for the lungs.
Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium; it passes through the bicuspid (mitral) valve to the left ventricle and leaves through the aorta for the body.
Diagram construction: Draw a heart outline 6 cm high and 5 cm wide, with the apex pointing downwards; divide it vertically into right and left sides with a septum.
In the upper half, draw and label two chambers, each about 2 cm wide: right atrium on the viewer’s left and left atrium on the viewer’s right.
In the lower half, draw and label two chambers, each about 2.5 cm wide: right ventricle on the viewer’s left and left ventricle on the viewer’s right; draw the left ventricle wall thicker.
Draw and label the tricuspid valve between the right atrium and right ventricle, and the bicuspid valve between the left atrium and left ventricle.

Draw the venae cavae entering the right atrium, the pulmonary artery leaving the right ventricle, the pulmonary veins entering the left atrium and the aorta leaving the left ventricle; add arrows to show the direction of blood flow.

written.text: What are Dark Reactions of Photosynthesis Mechanism? Write its events.
modelAnswer: Dark reactions, or the Calvin cycle, take place in the stroma of chloroplasts and do not require light directly.

PGA is reduced to PGAL using ATP and NADPH produced during the light reactions.
Some PGAL is used to make glucose and other carbohydrates.
The remaining PGAL is used to regenerate RuBP, allowing the cycle to continue.

written.text: Explain three main types of organisms in Kingdom Protista
modelAnswer: The three main types of organisms in Kingdom Protista are protozoans, algae and fungus-like protists.
Protozoans are animal-like and usually move to obtain food; examples include Amoeba and Paramecium.
Algae are plant-like and make food by photosynthesis; examples include Euglena and diatoms.
Fungus-like protists include slime molds and water molds; they commonly obtain food from organic matter.

written.text: Write a note on the Dark Reaction in detail
modelAnswer: The dark reaction, or Calvin cycle, occurs in the stroma of the chloroplast and does not require light directly.
Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP, forming PGA; this step is called carbon fixation.
ATP and NADPH made during the light reaction provide energy and hydrogen to convert PGA into PGAL.
Some PGAL is used to make glucose and other carbohydrates.
The remaining PGAL regenerates RuBP, allowing the cycle to continue.
written.followUp: Explain how carbon dioxide is converted into carbohydrate during the Calvin cycle.

rubric.why: The reactions occur in the chloroplast stroma and do not use light directly.
rubric.description: Gives the location and light requirement of the dark reaction.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that carbon dioxide is fixed to RuBP and forms PGA.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that PGAL forms carbohydrate and/or that RuBP is regenerated.

written.text: Explain digestion in small intestine in detail
modelAnswer: In the small intestine, bile from the liver neutralizes acidic chyme and emulsifies fats into small droplets.
Pancreatic juice enters the small intestine: amylase digests starch, trypsin digests proteins, and lipase digests fats.
Intestinal juice completes digestion: carbohydrates become glucose, proteins become amino acids, and fats become fatty acids and glycerol.
The digested nutrients are absorbed through the villi of the small intestine into the blood or lymph.

modelAnswer: Organisms are cellularly organized as unicellular or multicellular.

modelAnswer: Anaerobic respiration is the incomplete breakdown of glucose to release energy in the absence of oxygen.
In alcoholic fermentation, yeast converts glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide, releasing energy.
In lactic acid fermentation, glucose is converted into lactic acid, releasing energy; this occurs in muscle cells when oxygen is insufficient and in some bacteria.

It stores excess glucose as glycogen and releases glucose when needed.

written.text: Write a note on red blood cells and white blood cells
modelAnswer: Red blood cells (RBCs) contain haemoglobin, which gives them their red colour.
Mature human RBCs are biconcave and lack a nucleus; they transport oxygen in the blood.
White blood cells (WBCs) have a nucleus and do not contain haemoglobin.
WBCs protect the body against infection by engulfing pathogens or by producing antibodies.
RBCs are far more numerous than WBCs; RBCs are formed in bone marrow and live for about 120 days.

modelAnswer: Repeated mitotic cell division in the body wall of Hydra forms a small outgrowth called a bud.

written.text: Define fermentation. Write down the names of its two types.
modelAnswer: Fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose, releasing a small amount of energy.

written.text: What are dark reactions?
modelAnswer: Dark reactions are the light-independent reactions of photosynthesis; they do not require light directly.

written.text: Differentiate between intracellular enzymes and extra cellular enzymes.
modelAnswer: Intracellular enzymes remain and act inside the cell, for example enzymes involved in cellular respiration.

written.text: Write down a note on population level and community level.
modelAnswer: Population level: A population is a group of individuals of the same species living in the same area at the same time.

Community level: A community consists of the populations of different species living in the same area.

written.text: Write down the importance of biodiversity in detail.
modelAnswer: Biodiversity provides useful resources, including food, medicines, fuel, clothing and raw materials.

written.text: Write down two characteristics of hypothesis.
modelAnswer: A hypothesis is a tentative explanation for an observation or problem.

written.text: What are plasmodesmata?
modelAnswer: Plasmodesmata are microscopic channels that pass through the cell walls of adjacent plant cells.

written.text: Write down difference between somatic cells and germ line cells.
modelAnswer: Somatic cells are the ordinary body cells; germ line cells are cells that give rise to gametes.

modelAnswer: At the molecular level, atoms combine through chemical bonds to form molecules such as water, proteins and DNA.

written.text: Write down a note on status of viruses.
modelAnswer: Viruses are acellular and have no cellular structure or independent metabolism.
Outside a host cell, they are inactive and cannot reproduce; they can even be crystallized.

written.text: Define light reactions and write down the summary of events of light reactions.

Chlorophyll absorbs light energy and the excited electrons pass through an electron transport system.
Water is split (photolysis), releasing oxygen and supplying hydrogen and electrons.

written.text: How does "cohesion-tension theory" explain the transport of water in plants?
modelAnswer: Water evaporates from leaf surfaces and exits mainly through the stomata, producing transpiration pull or tension.
This tension pulls water upward through the xylem from the roots towards the leaves.
Cohesion between water molecules keeps them joined in a continuous column.
Adhesion between water molecules and the xylem walls helps support this column.
Thus, water is transported passively, without direct expenditure of energy by the plant.

written.text: How does transport of food occur in plants? Explain.
modelAnswer: Food is transported through the phloem by a process called translocation.

This pressure moves phloem sap towards sinks, such as roots or growing parts, where sugars are unloaded; water can return to the xylem.

written.text: Describe Pressureflow theory in detail.
modelAnswer: At a source, such as a leaf, sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem sieve tubes.
The increased sugar concentration lowers the water potential in the phloem, so water enters from the xylem by osmosis.
This raises the hydrostatic pressure in the phloem at the source.
The pressure difference drives phloem sap in bulk from the source towards a sink, such as a root or growing region.
At the sink, sugar is unloaded for use or storage; water leaves the phloem and returns to the xylem, reducing pressure there.

written.text: Describe summary of the events of light reactions with diagram.
modelAnswer: Chlorophyll in photosystems absorbs light energy.

Light excites electrons again in photosystem I; the electrons and hydrogen are used to reduce NADP to NADPH.
ATP and NADPH are used in the light-independent reactions; oxygen is released.

The valves prevent the backward flow of blood.

written.text: What is biodiversity? Give importance of biodiversity.
modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms found in an area or on Earth.
It helps maintain ecological balance and stable ecosystems.
It provides useful resources such as food, medicines, and raw materials.
It also supports important services such as pollination and nutrient cycling.
written.followUp: State three ways biodiversity benefits humans and ecosystems.

written.text: Describe events in dark reactions in detail.
modelAnswer: The dark reactions, also called the Calvin cycle, take place in the stroma of the chloroplast and do not directly require light.
Carbon dioxide combines with the five-carbon compound ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP), forming an unstable six-carbon compound.
The unstable compound immediately splits into molecules of phosphoglycerate (PGA), a three-carbon compound.
Using ATP and NADPH produced in the light reactions, PGA is reduced to phosphoglyceraldehyde (PGAL).
Some PGAL is used to form glucose and other carbohydrates; the remaining PGAL is used, with energy from ATP, to regenerate RuBP.
written.followUp: Describe the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: The dark reactions take place in the stroma of chloroplasts.
rubric.description: Identifies the site of the dark reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they occur in the chloroplast stroma.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is fixed by combining with the five-carbon acceptor RuBP.
rubric.description: Describes the initial fixation of carbon dioxide onto RuBP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying carbon dioxide and RuBP as reactants in fixation.

rubric.why: The unstable six-carbon product breaks down into molecules of PGA.
rubric.description: Names PGA as the first stable product of carbon fixation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying PGA (phosphoglycerate) as the product.

rubric.why: ATP and NADPH from the light reactions provide energy and reducing power to convert PGA to PGAL.
rubric.description: Explains the reduction of PGA to PGAL using products of the light reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking ATP and NADPH (or reduced NADP) with the conversion to PGAL.

rubric.why: Some PGAL is used to form carbohydrates, while the remainder regenerates the carbon dioxide acceptor.
rubric.description: Describes the fates of PGAL, including carbohydrate formation and regeneration of RuBP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that PGAL contributes to glucose formation and that remaining material regenerates RuBP.

written.text: Write a note on Dietary fibers in detail?
modelAnswer: Dietary fibres, also called roughage, are the indigestible parts of plant foods.
They include cellulose, hemicellulose and pectin and are found in fruits, vegetables and whole grains.
Fibre adds bulk to the faeces and helps move food through the digestive tract by promoting peristalsis.
It helps prevent constipation and supports regular bowel movements.
written.followUp: What are dietary fibres, and how do they help maintain a healthy digestive system?

rubric.why: Identifies dietary fibre as roughage that humans cannot digest.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct effect on bowel function.

written.text: Define Transpiration and write its significance?
modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
It cools the plant.
It creates a transpiration pull that helps in the upward movement of water.
It helps transport and distribute mineral salts through the plant.

rubric.description: States that transpiration helps transport or distribute mineral salts through the plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking transpiration with mineral-salt movement.

written.text: Differentiate between simple community and complex community.
modelAnswer: A simple community has relatively few species and relatively simple interactions among its organisms.
A complex community has many species and more varied, intricate interactions among its organisms.

written.text: Why do welts appear after mosquito bite?

written.text: Define photosynthesis. Explain dark reactions of photosynthesis.

They use ATP and NADPH produced during the light reactions to fix carbon dioxide.
Carbon dioxide combines with RuBP and is converted through intermediate compounds, including PGA and PGAL.
Some PGAL is used to form glucose, while the remaining material regenerates RuBP.

written.text: Describe summary of events of light reactions with the help of diagram.
modelAnswer: Light is absorbed by chlorophyll in photosystem II (PSII), exciting electrons.
Water undergoes photolysis, releasing electrons, hydrogen ions and oxygen.
The electrons pass along an electron transport chain; their energy is used to make ATP.
Light excites electrons again in photosystem I (PSI); these electrons help reduce NADP to NADPH.
Diagram: Light → PSII → electron transport chain → PSI → NADP⁺ → NADPH; H₂O → PSII (electrons and H⁺) and O₂ is released; electron transport drives ADP + Pi → ATP.

rubric.how: Give one mark for photolysis or its products.

written.text: Describe the sources, importance and effects of deficiency of iron and calcium.
modelAnswer: Iron is obtained from foods such as meat, liver, egg yolk and green vegetables.
Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in the blood; deficiency can cause anaemia and weakness.
Calcium is obtained from milk and other dairy foods, fish and eggs.
Calcium is needed for strong bones and teeth; its deficiency can cause rickets or weak bones.

written.text: Write down a note on mechanism of opening and closing of stomata and draw figure.
modelAnswer: In light, starch in the guard cells is converted into soluble sugar, increasing their osmotic pressure.
Water enters the guard cells by osmosis, making them turgid; they bend apart and the stomatal pore opens.
In darkness, soluble sugar changes back into starch and the osmotic pressure falls.
Water leaves the guard cells by osmosis, making them flaccid; the pore closes.

Figure construction: draw a diagram 6 cm high and 4 cm wide, with two kidney-shaped guard cells facing each other around an open pore; show thicker inner walls beside the pore and thinner outer walls.
Add several small chloroplasts inside each guard cell; label guard cell, stomatal pore, thick inner wall and thin outer wall.
written.followUp: Explain how the opening and closing of stomata help regulate water loss in plants.

rubric.why: Explains the change that draws water into guard cells and makes them turgid.
rubric.description: Guard cells become turgid
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that sugar formation or accumulation raises osmotic pressure, so water enters the guard cells.

rubric.why: Connects turgidity with stomatal opening.
rubric.description: Opening
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that turgid guard cells curve apart and open the stomatal pore.

rubric.why: Explains the loss of water and resulting closure.
rubric.description: Closing
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that sugar changes to starch or osmotic pressure falls, water leaves, and guard cells become flaccid.

rubric.why: Requires a recognisable, correctly labelled stomatal diagram.
rubric.description: Diagram: main parts
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for drawing two guard cells around a stomatal pore and labelling the guard cells and pore.

rubric.why: Checks key structural details in the drawing.
rubric.description: Diagram: structural detail
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for showing the thicker inner walls facing the pore and thinner outer walls, or for including chloroplasts and clear labels.

written.text: What is meant by “Control” in experiments?
modelAnswer: A control is the standard setup in an experiment used for comparison with the experimental setup.
The tested factor is absent from the control, while other conditions are kept the same, so the effect of that factor can be identified.

modelAnswer: A law is a hypothesis or scientific statement that has been repeatedly tested and not disproved.

written.text: Describe function of lysosomes.

They break down worn-out cell organelles, cellular waste and foreign particles.

written.text: Why viruses are not included in any of five kingdoms?
modelAnswer: Viruses are not included in any of the five kingdoms because they are acellular.
They cannot reproduce or carry out metabolism independently and multiply only inside a living host cell.

written.text: Write down the role of mitosis in regeneration.
modelAnswer: Mitosis produces new cells at the site of injury or loss.
These cells replace damaged or lost cells and help regenerate the body part.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that new cells replace lost or damaged cells or restore the body part.

written.text: Explain population level and community level.

written.text: Explain structure and function of cell membrane and also draw the diagram.
modelAnswer: The cell membrane is a thin, flexible boundary around the cell, made mainly of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it.
It is selectively permeable and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

written.text: What is meant by aerobic respiration? Explain its three main stages.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm: one glucose molecule is split into two pyruvic acid molecules, with a small amount of ATP produced.
The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondria: products derived from pyruvate are oxidized, carbon dioxide is released, and energy is transferred to electron carriers.
The electron transport chain occurs on the inner mitochondrial membrane: electrons pass along carriers, oxygen is the final electron acceptor and forms water, and most ATP is produced.
written.followUp: What is anaerobic respiration? State where it occurs in a cell.

rubric.why: Defines aerobic respiration by its use of oxygen and release of energy.
rubric.description: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for glucose breakdown using oxygen and releasing energy.

rubric.why: Glycolysis is the first stage and produces pyruvate in the cytoplasm.
rubric.description: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and splits glucose into two pyruvic acid molecules, producing a small amount of ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the location and principal product, or an equivalent correct description of glycolysis.

rubric.why: The Krebs cycle oxidizes products of glycolysis and releases carbon dioxide and electron carriers.
rubric.description: The Krebs cycle occurs in the mitochondria and releases carbon dioxide while transferring energy to electron carriers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct Krebs-cycle account, including location or key products.

rubric.why: The electron transport chain uses oxygen as the final electron acceptor and produces most ATP.
rubric.description: The electron transport chain operates on the inner mitochondrial membrane; oxygen accepts electrons and combines with hydrogen to form water, and most ATP is produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the chain’s location/role and 1 mark for oxygen forming water or production of most ATP.

written.text: What are the environmental hazards related to the use of fertilizers?
modelAnswer: Rain may wash excess fertilizers from fields into rivers and lakes.
The added nutrients can cause eutrophication and excessive algal growth.
When the algae die, their decomposition uses dissolved oxygen; oxygen depletion can kill fish and other aquatic life.
Nitrates may also leach into groundwater, while excessive fertilizer use can damage soil through acidification or salinity.
written.followUp: Explain how excessive pesticide use can harm an ecosystem.

rubric.why: Runoff transfers excess nutrients from fields into waterways.
rubric.description: Rain can wash fertilizers into rivers and lakes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing fertilizer runoff into surface water.

rubric.why: Excess nutrients promote eutrophication and algal blooms.
rubric.description: Nutrient enrichment causes excessive algal growth (eutrophication).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for eutrophication or excessive algal growth.

rubric.why: Decomposition of excess algae reduces dissolved oxygen and harms aquatic organisms.
rubric.description: When algae die and decompose, dissolved oxygen falls, which can kill fish and other aquatic organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for oxygen depletion or its effect on aquatic life.

rubric.why: Excess fertilizer can also contaminate groundwater or damage soil.
rubric.description: Nitrates may leach into groundwater, and excessive fertilizer use can contribute to soil acidification or salinity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for nitrate contamination or a valid soil-related hazard.

written.text: Define transpiration and describe factors which affect the rate of transpiration, in detail.
modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of leaves.
Light: greater light intensity usually opens stomata and increases the rate of transpiration.
Temperature: higher temperature increases evaporation and usually increases transpiration.
Humidity: high humidity decreases transpiration, while dry air increases it.
Wind: moving air carries moist air away from the leaf and usually increases transpiration.
Soil water: adequate water supports transpiration, while water shortage causes stomata to close and reduces the rate.
written.followUp: Define translocation and name the plant tissue through which it occurs.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining transpiration as water-vapour loss from the plant.

rubric.why: Light promotes stomatal opening, while higher temperature increases evaporation; both generally raise the rate of transpiration.
rubric.description: Explains the effects of light and temperature on transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that greater light intensity opens stomata and increases transpiration, and 1 mark for stating that higher temperature increases evaporation and transpiration.

rubric.why: Humidity affects the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and the surrounding air.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of humidity.

rubric.why: Wind carries moist air away from the leaf, while water availability affects stomatal opening and water loss.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing either the effect of wind or the effect of water availability.

written.text: What is mechanism of enzyme action? Give its equation.
modelAnswer: The substrate binds to the specific active site of an enzyme, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
The enzyme converts the substrate into product(s), which are released; the enzyme remains unchanged.
Equation: E + S ⇌ ES → E + P (E = enzyme, S = substrate, ES = enzyme-substrate complex, P = product).

rubric.why: Identifies how the substrate binds to the enzyme and forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.description: Substrate binds at the enzyme’s active site, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the binding and complex formation.

rubric.why: Shows the reaction sequence and that the enzyme is available again after the reaction.
rubric.description: Gives the equation E + S ⇌ ES → E + P and indicates that the enzyme remains unchanged.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equation or an equivalent correctly labelled sequence.

written.text: Differentiate between insoluble dietary fibres and soluble dietary fibres.
modelAnswer: Insoluble dietary fibre, such as cellulose, does not dissolve in water; it adds bulk to faeces and helps movement through the intestine.

written.text: Define plastids and explain its types with diagram.

Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments and give colour to flowers and fruits.

written.text: Who proposed five kingdom system? Explain kingdom protista and fungi.
modelAnswer: The five-kingdom system was proposed by Robert Whittaker in 1969.
Kingdom Protista includes mostly unicellular eukaryotes; many are aquatic, and they may be autotrophic or heterotrophic. Examples include Amoeba and Paramecium.

Kingdom Fungi consists of eukaryotic heterotrophs that absorb nutrients from their surroundings; most are multicellular, have chitin cell walls and form thread-like hyphae that make a mycelium. Yeast is a unicellular fungus.

written.text: Explain the percentage composition of blood plasma and draw diagram.

From the end of that sector, mark a 25.2° sector labelled Proteins (7%); the remaining 10.8° sector is labelled Other solutes (3%).
Add the title “Percentage composition of blood plasma.”
Diagram (not to scale): Water 90% | Proteins 7% | Other solutes 3%.

written.text: Describe pressure flow mechanism in detail.
modelAnswer: At the source, such as a leaf, sucrose is actively loaded into the phloem.
Water enters the phloem from the xylem by osmosis, raising the hydrostatic pressure at the source.
The pressure difference causes phloem sap to flow by mass flow towards a sink.
At the sink, sugars are unloaded and are used or stored.
Water leaves the phloem and returns to the xylem, so pressure is lower at the sink.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sugars are unloaded at the sink and used or stored.

written.text: Write a detailed note on Taxonomic Hierarchy.
modelAnswer: Taxonomic hierarchy is the arrangement of organisms into successive categories, from the smallest to the largest.
The categories in ascending order are species, genus, family, order, class, phylum and kingdom.
Species is the basic unit of classification and consists of similar organisms that can interbreed.
A genus contains related species; each successively higher category groups related members of the category below it.

written.text: Define Photosynthesis. Write a detailed note on light reactions of Photosynthesis.

Light reactions take place on the thylakoid membranes of the grana in chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
This energy splits water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen; this process is called photolysis.
Oxygen is released, while ATP and NADPH are formed for use in the next stage of photosynthesis.

written.text: Define Transpiration. Explain factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of leaves.
High temperature increases evaporation and usually increases the rate of transpiration.
High humidity decreases transpiration because the water-vapour gradient between the leaf and air is reduced.
Wind generally increases transpiration by carrying away moist air from around the leaf.
Light usually increases transpiration because stomata open; a larger leaf area or more stomata can also increase the rate.

written.text: Explain differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells have no membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic cells have a true, membrane-bound nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotic cells contain them.
Prokaryotic DNA is usually circular and lies in the nucleoid; eukaryotic DNA is arranged in linear chromosomes inside the nucleus.
Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller, about 1–10 µm, while eukaryotic cells are generally larger, about 10–100 µm.
Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes; eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes in their cytoplasm.

written.text: Write a detailed note on Kingdom Fungi and Kingdom Protista.
modelAnswer: Kingdom Fungi consists of eukaryotic organisms that lack chlorophyll and absorb nutrients from their surroundings; their cell walls contain chitin.
Many fungi are made of hyphae forming a mycelium and reproduce by spores; examples include moulds, mushrooms and yeast.
Kingdom Protista consists of eukaryotic organisms, most of which are unicellular; examples include Amoeba and Paramecium.
Protists are diverse: algae may make food by photosynthesis, while protozoans are heterotrophic; many live in aquatic or moist environments.

written.text: What is Anaerobic Respiration? Give its types in detail.
modelAnswer: Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose to release energy in the absence of oxygen; glucose is incompletely broken down and yields less energy than aerobic respiration.
Its two main types are alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.
In alcoholic fermentation, as in yeast, glucose produces ethanol, carbon dioxide and a small amount of energy: glucose → 2 ethanol + 2 carbon dioxide + energy.
In lactic acid fermentation, as in muscle cells when oxygen is insufficient, glucose produces lactic acid and a small amount of energy: glucose → 2 lactic acid + energy.
Lactic acid fermentation also occurs in some bacteria, such as Lactobacillus.

written.text: Describe the structure and function of stomach.
modelAnswer: The stomach is a J-shaped, muscular sac in the upper abdomen, below the diaphragm; it connects the oesophagus to the duodenum.
The cardiac sphincter controls the entry of food from the oesophagus, and the pyloric sphincter controls its passage into the duodenum.
Gastric glands in the stomach wall secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid, pepsinogen and protective mucus.
The stomach stores and churns food; its acidic juice helps kill microbes, and pepsin begins the digestion of proteins.

written.text: How would you relate the internal structure of root with the uptake of water and salts?
modelAnswer: Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells; their thin walls and large surface area provide an effective surface for absorbing water and mineral salts.
Water enters the root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis because the cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water.
Mineral ions are absorbed by root hairs, often by active transport against their concentration gradient using energy.
Water and ions then move through the cortex and endodermis towards the vascular tissue of the root.
They enter the xylem, which transports water and mineral salts upwards through the plant.

written.text: How do mitosis is significant for growth and development?

written.text: Define biology and from which the word biology is derived?

written.text: Define light reactions. And write the summary of events of light reactions.
modelAnswer: Light reactions are the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis and take place in the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, exciting its electrons.
Water molecules split by photolysis, providing hydrogen and releasing oxygen.
Oxygen is released as a by-product.
The absorbed energy is used to form ATP and reduced NADP (NADPH).

rubric.why: Defines the light reactions by their dependence on light.

rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy and its electrons become excited.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for chlorophyll absorbing light or exciting electrons.

rubric.why: Includes the splitting of water in the light reactions.
rubric.description: Water is split into hydrogen and oxygen (photolysis).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water is split.

rubric.why: Identifies oxygen as a product of water splitting.
rubric.description: Oxygen is released as a by-product.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for oxygen release.

rubric.why: Identifies the energy-rich products formed for the next stage of photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Light energy is used to form ATP and reduced NADP (NADPH).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both ATP and NADPH (reduced NADP).

written.text: What is fluid mosaic model.

written.text: What is exocytosis? Give its importance.
modelAnswer: Exocytosis is the process in which a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane and releases its contents outside the cell.

written.text: Explain the Pressure-Flow Mechanism for the transport of food in plants.
modelAnswer: Leaves are sources because they produce sugars, mainly sucrose, by photosynthesis.
Sucrose is actively loaded into the sieve tubes of the phloem at the source.
The increased solute concentration draws water from the xylem into the phloem by osmosis, raising the pressure in the sieve tubes.
At sinks, such as roots, fruits or storage organs, sugars are unloaded and used or stored; pressure is lower there.
This pressure difference drives the bulk flow of phloem sap from source to sink; water can return to the xylem.

Benign tumours remain localized and do not invade or spread to other parts of the body.
written.followUp: How do malignant tumours differ from benign tumours in their growth and spread?

rubric.description: Malignant tumours invade nearby tissues and can spread to other parts of the body.

rubric.description: Benign tumours remain localized and do not invade or spread to other parts of the body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that benign tumours do not invade or spread.

written.text: Define chromosomes.
modelAnswer: Chromosomes are thread-like structures found in the nucleus of a cell.
They consist of DNA associated with proteins and carry genes.
written.followUp: What are genes, and where are they found in a cell?

rubric.why: Gives the characteristic structure of chromosomes.
rubric.description: Chromosomes are thread-like structures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing their thread-like form.

rubric.why: Identifies their location and genetic material.
rubric.description: Chromosomes are found in the nucleus and consist of DNA associated with proteins; they carry genes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly locating chromosomes in the nucleus and linking them to DNA or genes.

written.text: What do you mean by photosystem?
modelAnswer: A photosystem is a group of chlorophyll and accessory pigment molecules associated with proteins.
Photosystems are present in the thylakoid membranes, where they capture light energy for photosynthesis.
written.followUp: Where are photosystems found, and what role do they perform in photosynthesis?

rubric.why: Identifies the pigment-and-protein components of a photosystem.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the location or light-capturing role.

written.text: Define ATP.
modelAnswer: ATP stands for adenosine triphosphate.
It is made up of adenine, ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
ATP is the energy currency of the cell; energy is released when its terminal phosphate bond is broken.
written.followUp: What is the role of ATP in cellular activities?

rubric.why: Identifies ATP and its main biological role.
rubric.description: Names ATP and states that it is the cell’s energy currency.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for expanding ATP as adenosine triphosphate and identifying it as the energy currency of the cell.

rubric.why: Shows knowledge of the components of an ATP molecule.
rubric.description: States that ATP consists of adenine, ribose and three phosphate groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly naming the three components.

written.text: Define biocatalysts and write two benefits of biocatalysts.
modelAnswer: Biocatalysts are biological catalysts, usually enzymes, that increase the rate of biochemical reactions.
They work efficiently under mild conditions in living cells.
They are highly specific and are not used up in the reactions they catalyse.
written.followUp: What are enzymes? Give two examples of reactions in which they act as biocatalysts.

accept: increase the rate of biochemical reactions
rubric.why: Tests the definition of biocatalysts.
rubric.description: Defines biocatalysts as biological substances, usually enzymes, that speed up biochemical reactions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as biological catalysts or stating that they speed up biochemical reactions.

rubric.why: Tests benefits of using biocatalysts.
rubric.description: Gives two benefits, such as working under mild conditions, being highly specific, remaining unchanged after reactions, or lowering activation energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two correct benefits.

written.text: Define the specificity of enzyme. Give an example.
modelAnswer: Enzyme specificity is the ability of an enzyme to act on a particular substrate because its active site fits that substrate.
For example, urease acts on urea.
written.followUp: What is enzyme-substrate specificity? Give an example of an enzyme and its substrate.

rubric.why: Tests the meaning of enzyme specificity.
rubric.description: Explains that an enzyme acts on only a particular substrate or a limited range of substrates.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an enzyme is specific to its substrate.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correctly matched enzyme and substrate.

written.text: What is meant by Villii? Write down its function.
modelAnswer: Villi are numerous finger like projections of the lining of the small intestine.
They increase the surface area and help absorb digested nutrients into the blood and lymph.
written.followUp: What are microvilli, and how do they help in absorption?

rubric.why: Tests the meaning and location of villi.
rubric.description: Defines villi as finger-like projections of the lining of the small intestine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing their finger-like shape and location in the small intestine.

rubric.why: Tests the function of villi.
rubric.description: States that villi increase the surface area for absorption of digested food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating their role in absorption or increasing surface area for absorption.

written.text: Explain relationship of biology with five other branches of science.
modelAnswer: Biology is related to physics through biophysics, which applies physical principles to living organisms and their processes.
Biology is related to chemistry through biochemistry, which studies the chemical substances and reactions in living organisms.
Biology is related to mathematics through biometry or biomathematics, which uses mathematical methods to measure and analyse biological data.
Biology is related to geography through biogeography, which studies the distribution of organisms in different regions.
Biology is related to economics through bioeconomics, which studies the economic use and value of biological resources.
written.followUp: Explain how biology is related to physics, chemistry, mathematics, geography and economics.

rubric.why: Tests the link between biology and physics.
rubric.description: Names biophysics and explains that it applies principles of physics to biological processes or structures.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct branch and its relevant connection to physics.

rubric.why: Tests the link between biology and chemistry.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct branch and its relevant connection to chemistry.

rubric.why: Tests the link between biology and mathematics.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct branch and its relevant connection to mathematics.

rubric.why: Tests the link between biology and geography.
rubric.description: Names biogeography and explains that it studies the geographical distribution of organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct branch and its relevant connection to geography.

rubric.why: Tests the link between biology and economics.
rubric.description: Names bioeconomics and explains that it considers the economic use or value of biological resources.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct branch and its relevant connection to economics.

written.text: Write a note on endocytosis. Explain your answer with labelled diagram.
modelAnswer: Endocytosis is the process by which a cell takes in substances from outside by folding its plasma membrane inward.
The membrane surrounds the substance and pinches off inside the cell to form a vesicle.
Phagocytosis is the uptake of solid particles; pinocytosis is the uptake of liquids.

Diagram construction: draw and label an external particle beside the cell; draw the cell membrane folding inward around it; show the membrane edges joining to enclose the particle in a vesicle inside the cytoplasm.
Labels: external particle; plasma membrane; inward fold; vesicle; cytoplasm.

rubric.description: Defines endocytosis as the uptake of substances into a cell by inward folding of the plasma membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing cellular uptake and membrane invagination.

rubric.why: Tests how material is enclosed and the main forms of endocytosis.
rubric.description: States that the membrane encloses material in a vesicle and/or correctly describes phagocytosis or pinocytosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct vesicle description or a correct type with what it takes in.

rubric.why: Checks understanding of the two commonly described forms of endocytosis.
rubric.description: Correctly distinguishes phagocytosis (solid particles) from pinocytosis (liquids).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating both forms and what each takes in.

written.text: Define the term "Extinct" and explain about endangered species of Pakistan.
modelAnswer: A species is extinct when no living members remain anywhere in the world.
An endangered species is one that is at serious risk of becoming extinct.
Threatened wildlife in Pakistan includes the Indus river dolphin, snow leopard, houbara bustard and green sea turtle.
Habitat destruction, hunting and pollution can reduce their populations.
Protecting habitats and preventing illegal hunting help conserve these species.
written.followUp: Define endangered species and name three threatened animal species found in Pakistan.

rubric.description: Explains that an endangered species faces a serious risk of extinction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing its risk of extinction.

rubric.why: Tests knowledge of threatened wildlife in Pakistan.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the Indus river dolphin.

rubric.why: Tests knowledge of another threatened species found in Pakistan.

written.text: Write a detailed note on electron transport chain.
modelAnswer: The electron transport chain is present in the inner mitochondrial membrane and consists of a series of electron carriers, including cytochromes.
NADH and FADH₂ donate electrons to the chain; as electrons pass from carrier to carrier, energy is released.
This energy pumps hydrogen ions across the inner membrane, creating a proton gradient.

Hydrogen ions flow back through ATP synthase, which uses the energy to make ATP from ADP and phosphate; oxygen is the final electron acceptor and combines with electrons and hydrogen ions to form water.
written.followUp: Explain how the proton gradient in mitochondria is used to produce ATP.

rubric.why: Identifies the location and the electron-carrier system of the chain.
rubric.description: Location and carriers
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the electron transport chain is on the inner mitochondrial membrane and involves electron carriers (such as cytochromes).

rubric.why: Shows that reduced coenzymes supply electrons to the chain.
rubric.description: Electron donors
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying NADH and/or FADH₂ as electron donors.

rubric.why: Connects proton movement through ATP synthase with ATP production.
rubric.description: ATP formation
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the proton gradient drives ATP synthase to form ATP from ADP and phosphate.

rubric.why: Identifies oxygen’s role at the end of the chain and the formation of water.
rubric.description: Final electron acceptor
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that oxygen accepts electrons (and hydrogen ions) to form water.

written.text: Describe the digestion of food in small intestine.
modelAnswer: Acidic food from the stomach enters the small intestine, where bile makes the contents alkaline and emulsifies fats into small droplets.
Pancreatic amylase changes starch into maltose.
Pancreatic trypsin breaks proteins into peptides.
Pancreatic lipase breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol.
Enzymes in intestinal juice complete digestion: maltase changes maltose into glucose, while peptidases change peptides into amino acids.
written.followUp: Describe the roles of bile and pancreatic juice in digestion in the small intestine.

rubric.why: States both important actions of bile in the small intestine.
rubric.description: Action of bile
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that bile helps neutralize acidic chyme and emulsifies fats.

rubric.why: Gives the substrate and product of pancreatic amylase.
rubric.description: Carbohydrate digestion
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that pancreatic amylase changes starch into maltose.

rubric.why: Gives the action of trypsin on proteins.
rubric.description: Protein digestion
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that trypsin breaks proteins into peptides.

rubric.why: Gives the products of fat digestion by lipase.
rubric.description: Fat digestion
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that lipase breaks fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

rubric.why: Describes completion of digestion by intestinal enzymes.
rubric.description: Completion of digestion
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that intestinal enzymes complete digestion, producing simple sugars such as glucose and amino acids.

written.text: Explain the composition and functions of white blood cells.
modelAnswer: White blood cells are colourless, nucleated cells and generally have an irregular shape.
They include granulocytes, such as neutrophils, and agranulocytes, such as lymphocytes and monocytes.
Some white blood cells engulf and digest pathogens by phagocytosis.
Lymphocytes produce antibodies, which help defend the body and provide immunity.
written.followUp: Describe how white blood cells protect the body against pathogens.

rubric.why: Describes basic structural features of white blood cells.
rubric.description: Composition and structure
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that white blood cells are colourless and nucleated; mention of their irregular shape is also acceptable.

rubric.why: Explains how some white blood cells destroy invading organisms.
rubric.description: Phagocytosis

rubric.why: Identifies antibody production as a defence function.
rubric.description: Antibody defence
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that white blood cells, especially lymphocytes, produce antibodies and help provide immunity.

written.text: Define bioeconomics.

written.text: State about Ibn Sina achievements in Biology.
modelAnswer: Ibn Sina, also known as Avicenna, was a famous Muslim physician and scholar.
He wrote Al-Qanun fi al-Tibb (The Canon of Medicine), which remained an important medical textbook for centuries.

written.text: Define scientific method.
modelAnswer: The scientific method is a systematic way of investigating and solving a scientific problem.
It involves making observations, forming a hypothesis, testing it by experiments and drawing a conclusion.

written.text: How phragmoplast is formed in plant cell?
modelAnswer: During telophase, microtubules between the daughter nuclei organise into a phragmoplast.
The phragmoplast guides Golgi-derived vesicles to the cell equator; the vesicles fuse to form the cell plate, which develops into a new cell wall.
written.followUp: Explain how the cell plate develops during cytokinesis in a plant cell.

rubric.why: Describes when and where the phragmoplast forms and identifies its basis.
rubric.description: Formation of phragmoplast
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that during telophase microtubules or spindle fibres form a phragmoplast between the daughter nuclei.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the phragmoplast guides vesicles to the equator, where they fuse to form the cell plate.

written.text: How mitosis helps in cell replacement of body?
modelAnswer: Mitosis produces new cells that are genetically identical to the original cell.
These cells replace worn-out or damaged body cells and help repair tissues.

rubric.why: The new cells replace body cells that are worn out or damaged.
rubric.description: Explains that new cells replace worn-out or damaged cells or help repair tissues.

written.text: What is meant by tetrad?
modelAnswer: A tetrad is formed during prophase I of meiosis when two homologous chromosomes pair.
The pair contains four chromatids in total.
written.followUp: How does mitosis help an organism grow?

rubric.why: A tetrad forms when homologous chromosomes pair during meiosis.
rubric.description: States that homologous chromosomes pair.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the pairing that forms a tetrad.

rubric.description: Identifies the four chromatids in a tetrad.

written.text: How photosynthesis gets effected by temperature?
modelAnswer: As temperature rises, the rate of photosynthesis increases up to an optimum because the reactions are enzyme-controlled.
Above the optimum, enzymes denature and the rate of photosynthesis decreases.
written.followUp: What happens to the rate of photosynthesis when temperature rises above its optimum?

rubric.description: States that the rate of photosynthesis increases up to an optimum temperature.
rubric.how: Award for describing the increase in rate before the optimum.

rubric.why: Above the optimum, photosynthetic enzymes denature and the rate falls.

written.text: How enzymes are used as biological detergent?
modelAnswer: Biological detergents contain enzymes that break down organic substances in stains, helping remove them during washing.
For example, proteases break down protein stains, and lipases break down fat stains.

written.text: What does saturation of active sites mean?
modelAnswer: Saturation of active sites means that substrate molecules are occupying all the active sites of the enzymes.
The reaction is then at its maximum rate, so adding more substrate does not increase the rate.

rubric.why: When all active sites are occupied, the enzyme is working at its maximum rate; extra substrate cannot increase the rate.
rubric.description: States the effect of saturation on reaction rate.
rubric.how: Award for noting that the rate is maximum or will not rise when more substrate is added.

written.text: Define “Lock & Key Model” of enzymes.
modelAnswer: The lock-and-key model states that an enzyme's active site has a specific shape that fits its substrate, like a key fitting a lock.
The substrate binds to form an enzyme-substrate complex, and products are released.

written.text: What is “Cohesion-Tension Theory”?
modelAnswer: The cohesion-tension theory states that transpiration from leaves creates tension in the xylem, pulling water upward.
Cohesion between water molecules maintains a continuous column of water from the roots to the leaves.
written.followUp: How does transpiration pull help water move up through xylem?

written.text: Define endangered species and discuss any three types of endangered species in Pakistan.

written.text: Write a note on aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose in the presence of oxygen to release energy.
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water + energy.
Anaerobic respiration is the breakdown of glucose without oxygen and releases less energy.
In muscles, glucose → lactic acid + energy; in yeast, glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide + energy.

written.text: Describe in detail Molecular level and Tissue level.
modelAnswer: At the molecular level, atoms combine to form molecules and large biological molecules such as proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids.
These molecules are the chemical components of cells and their structures.

The cells of a tissue perform a particular function.

written.text: Explain structure and function of cell membrane with the help of diagram.
modelAnswer: The cell membrane is a thin, flexible boundary that surrounds the cytoplasm and separates it from the external environment.

The membrane is selectively permeable and controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell.

written.text: Discuss light reaction of photosynthesis in detail.
modelAnswer: The light reaction occurs on the thylakoid membranes in the grana of chloroplasts.
Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, exciting electrons to a higher energy level.
Light energy splits water molecules by photolysis; oxygen is released, and hydrogen ions and electrons are produced.
The excited electrons pass through an electron transport chain, and their energy is used to make ATP by photophosphorylation.
Hydrogen and electrons reduce NADP to NADPH; ATP and NADPH are used in the light-independent reaction.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking chlorophyll with absorption of light.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for water splitting and oxygen production.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both ATP and NADPH, or equivalent accurate descriptions of their formation.

written.text: Describe the disorders of Gut in detail.
modelAnswer: Diarrhoea is the frequent passage of loose, watery stools. It causes excessive loss of water and salts and may lead to dehydration.

Appendicitis is inflammation of the appendix and commonly causes abdominal pain.

written.text: Define transpiration and discuss factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata of leaves.

High humidity decreases the rate because the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and air is smaller.
Wind generally increases the rate by carrying away moist air around the leaves.

Mucus protects the stomach lining from the acid and digestive enzymes.
Muscular contractions churn food with gastric juice to form chyme, which then passes into the small intestine.

written.text: Write summary of events of light reactions.
modelAnswer: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy, exciting its electrons.

NADP accepts electrons and protons to form NADPH; oxygen is released as a by-product.

rubric.how: Award for stating that ATP is formed.

written.text: Describe factors which affect the rate of transpiration.

Low humidity (dry air) increases the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and the air, increasing transpiration.
Wind removes the moist air around the leaf, maintaining the water-vapour gradient and increasing transpiration.
Light generally causes stomata to open, increasing transpiration; darkness usually reduces it as stomata close.
Adequate soil water allows continued water loss, whereas a shortage of soil water may cause stomata to close and reduce transpiration.

written.text: Describe any ten branches of biology.
modelAnswer: Morphology is the study of the form and external structure of organisms.
Anatomy is the study of the internal structure of organisms.
Histology is the study of tissues.
Cytology is the study of cells.
Physiology is the study of the functions of living organisms and their parts.
Genetics is the study of heredity and variation.
Taxonomy is the identification, naming, and classification of organisms.
Embryology is the study of the development of an embryo.
Ecology is the study of the relationships of organisms with one another and their environment.
Palaeontology is the study of fossils.
Microbiology is the study of microorganisms.
Parasitology is the study of parasites and their relationships with hosts.
Biotechnology is the use of organisms or biological processes for human benefit.

written.text: Define mitochondria? Explain it with the help of diagram.

The cristae provide a large surface area for reactions of cellular respiration, while the matrix contains enzymes involved in respiration.
Mitochondria are therefore called the powerhouses of the cell because they supply ATP for cellular activities.

written.text: Describe digestion and Absorption of food in small intestine.

The inner lining has villi that absorb digested nutrients; glucose and amino acids enter blood capillaries, while fatty acids and glycerol enter lacteals.
Blood and lymph carry the absorbed nutrients from the small intestine to the body cells.

written.text: Describe factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Temperature: A rise in temperature increases evaporation from leaf surfaces and generally increases transpiration.
Humidity: High humidity reduces transpiration because the difference in water-vapour concentration between the leaf and air is smaller; dry air increases it.
Wind: Wind removes moist air around the leaf, maintaining a steep diffusion gradient and generally increasing transpiration.
Light: Light usually causes stomata to open, increasing water loss; in darkness stomata tend to close and transpiration falls.
Water supply and leaf features also affect the rate: water shortage may cause stomata to close, while a larger leaf area generally allows more transpiration.
