rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the enzymes.

rubric.why: The enzymes digest food material into simpler substances, commonly after the lysosome joins a food vacuole.
rubric.description: Explains the breakdown of food material.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing digestion into simpler substances or lysosome fusion with a food vacuole.

written.text: How is the solute concentration helpful in opening and closing of stomata?
modelAnswer: When solute concentration in guard cells increases, water enters them by osmosis.
The guard cells become turgid and the stomata open.
When solutes and water leave, the guard cells become flaccid and the stomata close.
written.followUp: Explain how water movement in guard cells causes stomata to open and close.

rubric.why: An increase in guard-cell solutes draws water into the cells by osmosis, making them turgid and opening the stomata.
rubric.description: Explains how increased solute concentration leads to water uptake and opening of the stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the opening sequence: solutes increase, water enters, or guard cells become turgid and stomata open.

rubric.why: When guard cells lose solutes and water, they become flaccid and the stomata close.
rubric.description: Explains how solute and water loss leads to closure of the stomata.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the closing sequence: solutes or water leave, guard cells become flaccid, or stomata close.

written.text: How can you divide five kingdoms into two groups on the basis of types of cells?
modelAnswer: The kingdom Monera has prokaryotic cells.
The kingdoms Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia have eukaryotic cells.
written.followUp: Name the kingdoms that contain prokaryotic cells and those that contain eukaryotic cells.

rubric.why: Monera is the prokaryotic kingdom in the five-kingdom classification.
rubric.description: Places Monera in the prokaryotic group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming Monera as the group with prokaryotic cells.

rubric.why: The other four kingdoms have eukaryotic cells.
rubric.description: Identifies the eukaryotic kingdoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the four eukaryotic kingdoms, or for clearly identifying them as the kingdoms other than Monera.

written.text: Give two characteristics of Kingdom Protista.
modelAnswer: Protists are eukaryotic organisms, with a true nucleus.
Most protists are unicellular.
written.followUp: State two characteristics of Kingdom Fungi.

rubric.why: Kingdom Protista consists of eukaryotic organisms.
rubric.description: Identifies Protista as eukaryotic.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that protists have a true nucleus or are eukaryotic.

rubric.why: Protists are commonly described as mostly unicellular; other textbook characteristics are also acceptable.
rubric.description: Gives one further characteristic of Protista.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they are mostly unicellular, aquatic, autotrophic, or heterotrophic.

written.text: Define the terms autotroph and heterotroph with one example each.
modelAnswer: An autotroph makes its own food; for example, a green plant.
A heterotroph obtains food from other organisms; for example, a human.
written.followUp: Give two characteristics of Kingdom Monera.

rubric.why: An autotroph makes its own food, usually using light energy.
rubric.description: Defines autotroph and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an autotroph makes its own food and giving a suitable example, such as a green plant.

rubric.why: A heterotroph obtains food from other organisms.
rubric.description: Defines heterotroph and gives an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a heterotroph obtains food from other organisms and giving a suitable example, such as a human or an animal.

written.text: Nucleus is visible only in interphase while chromosomes are only visible in the cell division stage. Why is that?
modelAnswer: During interphase, DNA is present as long, thin, uncoiled chromatin, so individual chromosomes cannot be seen distinctly.
During cell division, the chromatin condenses into short, thick chromosomes that become visible.
written.followUp: Why are chromosomes not distinctly visible during interphase?

rubric.why: During interphase, the genetic material is in a loose chromatin form rather than distinct chromosomes.
rubric.description: Explains why chromosomes are not distinct in interphase.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chromatin is loose, diffuse, or uncoiled during interphase.

rubric.why: During cell division, chromatin condenses into distinct chromosomes that can be seen.
rubric.description: Explains why chromosomes are visible during cell division.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes during division.

written.text: Write down two points in significance of mitosis.
modelAnswer: Mitosis increases the number of cells and enables growth.
It replaces damaged or worn-out cells and helps in asexual reproduction in some organisms.
written.followUp: State two roles of mitosis in living organisms.

rubric.why: Mitosis produces more cells for growth.
rubric.description: States that mitosis enables growth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking mitosis to growth or an increase in cell number.

rubric.why: Mitosis replaces damaged or worn-out cells and also supports asexual reproduction in some organisms.
rubric.description: States another significance of mitosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning repair, replacement of cells, or asexual reproduction.

written.text: What is meant by photosystem?
modelAnswer: A photosystem is a group of pigment molecules, including chlorophyll, arranged in the thylakoid membrane.
It absorbs light energy and transfers it to the reaction-centre chlorophyll.
written.followUp: What is the role of chlorophyll in a photosystem?

rubric.why: A photosystem is a group of photosynthetic pigments, including chlorophyll, arranged in the thylakoid membrane.
rubric.description: Identifies a photosystem as a pigment-containing unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is a group or cluster of pigments in the thylakoid membrane.

rubric.why: The pigments absorb light and pass the energy to the reaction centre.
rubric.description: States the light-absorption or energy-transfer role of a photosystem.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that it absorbs light energy and transfers it to the reaction centre.

written.text: Define fermentation and write the names of its two types.
modelAnswer: Fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose to release energy.
Its two types are alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.
written.followUp: Name the products of alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.

rubric.why: Fermentation is the anaerobic breakdown of glucose, releasing energy.
rubric.description: Defines fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing fermentation as the breakdown of glucose without oxygen, with energy release.

rubric.why: The two types are alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.
rubric.description: Names the two types of fermentation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both alcoholic fermentation and lactic acid fermentation.

written.text: Explain the function of enzyme.
modelAnswer: An enzyme is a biological catalyst.
It speeds up a biochemical reaction by lowering its activation energy and is not used up in the reaction.
written.followUp: What is an enzyme, and how does it affect the rate of a reaction?

rubric.why: An enzyme is a biological catalyst.
rubric.description: Identifies an enzyme as a catalyst.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying an enzyme as a biological catalyst.

rubric.why: Enzymes speed up reactions, commonly by lowering their activation energy.
rubric.description: States the effect of an enzyme on a reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an enzyme speeds up a reaction or lowers its activation energy.

written.text: Describe the function of Inhibitor.
modelAnswer: An inhibitor is a substance that decreases or stops the activity of an enzyme.
It may bind to the enzyme and block its active site, or change the enzyme's shape so the substrate cannot bind effectively.
written.followUp: How does an inhibitor affect an enzyme and its reaction?

rubric.why: An inhibitor reduces or prevents enzyme activity, slowing or stopping the reaction.
rubric.description: States the effect of an inhibitor on enzyme activity or reaction rate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an inhibitor decreases enzyme activity or slows or stops the reaction.

rubric.why: An inhibitor can block the active site or alter the enzyme's shape, preventing effective substrate binding.
rubric.description: Explains how an inhibitor interferes with enzyme action.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing an inhibitor binding to the enzyme and blocking the active site, preventing substrate binding, or changing the enzyme's shape.

written.text: How do plants get water and ions from soil?
modelAnswer: Root hairs provide a large surface area in contact with the soil.
Water enters root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis.
Mineral ions are absorbed by root cells by active transport, which requires energy.
Water and ions pass through the root tissues to the xylem for transport through the plant.
written.followUp: Explain how root hairs help a plant absorb water and mineral salts.

rubric.why: Identifies how roots are adapted for absorption.
rubric.description: Root hairs provide a large surface area for absorption from the soil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking root hairs with increased absorptive surface area.

rubric.why: States the process by which water enters root cells.
rubric.description: Water enters root-hair cells from the soil by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming osmosis as the process of water uptake.

rubric.why: States the process used to take up mineral ions.
rubric.description: Mineral ions are absorbed by root cells by active transport.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming active transport for mineral-ion uptake.

rubric.why: Recognizes that active uptake requires energy.
rubric.description: Active transport uses energy to move ions, often against their concentration gradient.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that energy is required for active transport or that ions can be taken up against their concentration gradient.

written.text: For the purpose of photosynthesis, chlorophyll and light are the basic needs. Explain.
modelAnswer: Chlorophyll in green plants absorbs light energy.
Light provides the energy required for photosynthesis.
The absorbed light energy is converted into chemical energy.
This energy is used to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
written.followUp: Describe the role of carbon dioxide and water in photosynthesis, and write the word equation.

rubric.why: Explains the role of chlorophyll.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorophyll absorbs light.

rubric.why: Explains why light is needed.
rubric.description: Light supplies the energy needed for photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying light as the energy source for photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Explains the conversion of energy during the process.
rubric.description: The absorbed light energy is converted into chemical energy stored in food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing conversion of light energy into chemical energy.

rubric.why: States the useful product made using the absorbed energy.
rubric.description: The chemical energy is used to make glucose (food) from carbon dioxide and water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying glucose or food as the product made in photosynthesis.

written.text: Write down the structure and types of plastids in plant cells.
modelAnswer: Plastids are membrane-bound organelles found in plant cells and are enclosed by a double membrane.
A chloroplast contains a fluid matrix called the stroma.
Its internal membrane sacs, called thylakoids, are arranged in stacks called grana and contain chlorophyll.
Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis; chromoplasts contain coloured pigments that give colour to plant parts.
Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food such as starch, oils or proteins.
written.followUp: Describe the structure of a chloroplast and state the functions of its main parts.

rubric.why: Describes the outer structure of plastids.
rubric.description: A plastid is enclosed by a double membrane.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that plastids have a double membrane.

rubric.why: Describes the internal structure of a chloroplast.
rubric.description: The stroma is the fluid matrix; thylakoids are arranged in stacks called grana.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the stroma, thylakoids and grana.

rubric.why: Names the function of chloroplasts.
rubric.description: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking chloroplasts with photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Names a plastid type and its characteristic contents or role.
rubric.description: Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments that give colour to plant parts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking chromoplasts with coloured pigments or colour.

rubric.why: Names a plastid type and its function.
rubric.description: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking leucoplasts with food storage.

written.text: Which are the major biological issues now a days?
modelAnswer: Major biological issues today include food shortage, disease, energy shortage and environmental pollution.
These issues affect human health, the availability of resources and the quality of the environment.
written.followUp: Name two biological problems faced by people today and briefly state their effects.

rubric.why: Identifies major biological issues.
rubric.description: Examples include food shortage, disease, energy shortage and environmental pollution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming two relevant biological issues.

rubric.why: Recognizes additional major biological issues.
rubric.description: Examples include food shortage, disease, energy shortage and environmental pollution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two further relevant issues, or for clearly explaining the importance of the named issues.

written.text: Discuss the tissue level with one example.
modelAnswer: At the tissue level, similar cells work together to perform the same function.
For example, muscle tissue is made of cells that contract and bring about movement.
written.followUp: What is an organ? Give one example of an organ and identify its tissues.

rubric.why: Defines tissue in terms of its cells and their work.
rubric.description: A tissue is a group of similar cells that perform the same function.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining a tissue as similar cells working together for a common function.

rubric.why: Illustrates the tissue level with an example and its function.
rubric.description: For example, muscle tissue consists of cells that contract and bring about movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct tissue example and its function.

written.text: How can you classify the biomolecules? Give their names with definition.
modelAnswer: Biomolecules are molecules present in living organisms.
They are classified into inorganic biomolecules, such as water and mineral salts, and organic biomolecules, such as carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids.
Organic biomolecules generally contain carbon, while inorganic biomolecules include substances such as water and mineral salts.
written.followUp: Name the major classes of organic biomolecules and give one example of each.

rubric.why: Defines biomolecules.
rubric.description: Biomolecules are molecules present in living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining biomolecules as molecules found in living organisms.

rubric.why: Classifies biomolecules into the two broad groups and identifies their distinction.
rubric.description: Biomolecules are classified as organic and inorganic; organic molecules generally contain carbon, while inorganic examples include water and mineral salts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both groups and giving a suitable distinguishing feature or example.

written.text: Define the term "Bioinformatics".
modelAnswer: Bioinformatics is the use of computer technology to collect, store, manage and analyse biological data.
written.followUp: What is meant by genomics?

rubric.why: Identifies the use of computers in bioinformatics.
rubric.description: Use of computer technology
rubric.how: Award for stating that computers or computer technology are used.

rubric.why: Identifies the information bioinformatics handles.
rubric.description: Handling biological data
rubric.how: Award for mentioning biological data or information.

written.text: How can we do reporting of our results after experiments?
modelAnswer: After experiments, results are organised and presented in a scientific report, often using tables or graphs.
The findings may then be published in scientific journals or presented at scientific meetings.
written.followUp: How may a scientist communicate the results of an investigation to other scientists?

rubric.why: Recognises that results can be organised and presented clearly.
rubric.description: Organising results
rubric.how: Award for mentioning a suitable presentation of results, such as tables, graphs, or a scientific report.

rubric.why: Identifies a way to share experimental findings with others.
rubric.description: Reporting or sharing findings
rubric.how: Award for stating that findings may be published or presented to the scientific community.

written.text: Define "Law". Give one example also.
modelAnswer: A scientific law is a uniform or constant fact of nature that describes the behaviour of natural phenomena.
An example is Mendel’s law of segregation.
written.followUp: Define a scientific theory and give one example.

rubric.why: Gives the essential meaning of a scientific law.
rubric.description: Definition of law
rubric.how: Award for describing a law as a uniform or constant fact of nature that describes natural phenomena.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a scientific law.
rubric.description: Example
rubric.how: Award for naming a relevant scientific law.

written.text: Write down the Fluid Mosaic Model of cell membrane.
modelAnswer: The cell membrane consists of a phospholipid bilayer with proteins embedded in it.
The lipids and some proteins can move within the membrane, giving it a fluid, mosaic arrangement.
written.followUp: Name the molecules that form the basic bilayer of the cell membrane.

rubric.why: Identifies the membrane’s basic structure.
rubric.description: Phospholipid bilayer
rubric.how: Award for stating that the cell membrane is made of a phospholipid bilayer.

rubric.why: Explains the mosaic and fluid features of the model.
rubric.description: Proteins and fluid arrangement
rubric.how: Award for describing proteins as embedded in the bilayer and/or able to move within it, producing a mosaic arrangement.

written.text: What is the role of Muslim scientist Abu-Usman Umer Aljahiz?
modelAnswer: Muslim scientist Abu-Usman Umer Al-Jahiz wrote Kitab al-Hayawan, meaning The Book of Animals.
It described animals and their lives, including their relationships with food and the environment.
written.followUp: Name the book written by Al-Jahiz and state what it was about.

rubric.why: Identifies Al-Jahiz’s major work.
rubric.description: Book written by Al-Jahiz
rubric.how: Award for naming Kitab al-Hayawan or translating its title as The Book of Animals.

rubric.why: States his contribution to the study of animals.
rubric.description: Contribution to zoology
rubric.how: Award for stating that the book described animals or their lives, including their relations with food or environment.

written.text: Differentiate between the two terms "Extinct" and "Endangered" used in classification.
modelAnswer: Extinct species have no living members and no longer exist.
Endangered species still exist but are at risk of becoming extinct.
written.followUp: Differentiate between a vulnerable species and an extinct species.

rubric.why: Defines the status of an extinct species.
rubric.description: Extinct
rubric.how: Award for stating that an extinct species has no living members or no longer exists.

rubric.why: Defines the status of an endangered species.
rubric.description: Endangered
rubric.how: Award for stating that an endangered species is at risk of extinction.

written.text: A nerve cell is not divided after its formation. In which phase of cell cycle is it?
modelAnswer: It is in the G0 phase of the cell cycle.
In this phase, the cell is not dividing.
written.followUp: What is the G0 phase of the cell cycle?

rubric.why: Names the phase in which the nerve cell remains.
rubric.description: Phase identification
rubric.how: Award for identifying the G0 phase.

rubric.why: States the defining cell state in this phase.
rubric.description: Non-dividing state
rubric.how: Award for stating that the cell is not dividing.

written.text: Plants do not make their gametes by meiosis. What is its reason?
modelAnswer: Plants show alternation of generations: the diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.
These spores grow into a haploid gametophyte, which produces gametes by mitosis.
written.followUp: Why do flowering plants produce spores by meiosis but form gametes by mitosis?

rubric.why: Meiosis in the diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores.
rubric.description: States that plants produce spores by meiosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking meiosis with spore production.

rubric.why: The haploid gametophyte forms gametes by mitosis.
rubric.description: States that plant gametes are formed by mitosis in the gametophyte.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking mitosis with gamete formation.

written.text: Who discovered ATP and who named it as an energy transfer molecule in the living cell?
modelAnswer: ATP was discovered by Karl Lohmann in 1929.
Fritz Lipmann named ATP as an energy-transfer molecule in the living cell.
written.followUp: Who discovered the role of ATP in muscle contraction, and who proposed its role in energy transfer in cells?

rubric.why: Karl Lohmann is credited with discovering ATP.
rubric.description: Names the discoverer of ATP.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Karl Lohmann.

rubric.why: Lipmann described ATP as an energy-transfer molecule in the living cell.
rubric.description: Names the scientist who proposed ATP's energy-transfer role.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for Lipmann.

written.text: Differentiate between oxidation and reduction reaction.
modelAnswer: Oxidation is the loss of electrons, addition of oxygen, or removal of hydrogen.
Reduction is the gain of electrons, removal of oxygen, or addition of hydrogen.
written.followUp: Differentiate between anabolism and catabolism.

rubric.why: Oxidation is commonly described by electron loss, oxygen gain, or hydrogen loss.
rubric.description: Gives a correct definition or characteristic of oxidation.

rubric.why: Reduction is commonly described by electron gain, oxygen loss, or hydrogen gain.
rubric.description: Gives a correct definition or characteristic of reduction.

written.text: Differentiate between Protease and Amylase enzyme.
modelAnswer: Protease breaks down proteins into peptides and ultimately amino acids.
Amylase breaks down starch into maltose.
written.followUp: State the substrates and products of lipase and maltase.

rubric.why: Proteases digest proteins into smaller peptides and ultimately amino acids.
rubric.description: States the action of protease on proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying proteins as the substrate and amino acids as the end product.

rubric.why: Amylase breaks starch down into maltose.
rubric.description: States the action of amylase on starch.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying starch as the substrate and maltose as the product.

written.text: Define minerals and write down the names of any two major minerals.
modelAnswer: Minerals are inorganic elements required by organisms to perform various functions.
Two major minerals are calcium and phosphorus.
written.followUp: Define trace minerals and name two examples.

rubric.why: Minerals are inorganic nutrients or elements needed by organisms.
rubric.description: Defines minerals as inorganic nutrients or elements required by organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition.

rubric.why: Calcium, phosphorus, potassium, sodium, and magnesium are examples of major minerals.
rubric.description: Names any two major minerals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two correct examples.

written.text: What is Pulmonary vein? What is its function?
modelAnswer: The pulmonary vein is a blood vessel that carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the left atrium of the heart.
Its function is to return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.
written.followUp: What is the function of the pulmonary artery?

rubric.why: The pulmonary vein returns oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart's left atrium.
rubric.description: States what blood the pulmonary vein carries and its route.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying oxygenated blood travelling from the lungs to the left atrium.

rubric.why: Its function is to deliver oxygenated blood to the left atrium.

written.text: Why do you think that transpiration is a necessary evil for plants?
modelAnswer: Transpiration is an evil because excessive loss of water may cause a plant to wilt.
It is necessary because it creates a transpiration pull that helps transport water and minerals from roots to leaves.
It also helps cool the plant.
written.followUp: Give two benefits of transpiration to a plant.

rubric.why: Transpiration can cause excessive water loss and wilting, so it is considered harmful.
rubric.description: Explains why transpiration is an evil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting harmful water loss or the risk of wilting.

rubric.why: Transpiration creates a pull that helps move water and minerals from roots to leaves.
rubric.description: Explains a necessary benefit of transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking transpiration with water/mineral transport or transpiration pull.

written.text: Write down a note on the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Light generally opens stomata and increases transpiration; darkness tends to reduce it.
Higher temperature increases evaporation and therefore increases transpiration.
High humidity reduces transpiration, while dry air increases it.
Wind increases transpiration by carrying away moist air around the leaf; a larger leaf area or more stomata also increases water loss, while a thick cuticle reduces it.
The availability of water in the soil also affects the rate: water shortage reduces transpiration.
written.followUp: Explain how humidity, wind, and light affect the rate of transpiration.

rubric.why: Light generally causes stomata to open, increasing water-vapour loss.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of light on transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that light increases transpiration, usually by opening stomata.

rubric.why: Higher temperature increases evaporation from leaf surfaces and raises transpiration.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of temperature on transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating that higher temperature increases the rate.

rubric.why: Humid air reduces the water-vapour gradient from leaf to air; dry air increases it.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of humidity on transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct effect of high humidity or dry air.

rubric.why: Wind removes moist air near the leaf, while leaf area and leaf structures also affect water loss.
rubric.description: Explains one other factor affecting transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct effect of wind or a leaf feature.

written.text: Write in detail the importance of biodiversity with respect to natural ecosystem with an example.
modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms in an ecosystem, and it helps maintain ecosystem balance and stability.
Different species are linked in food chains and food webs, so changes in one population can affect others.
A variety of organisms also supports essential processes such as nutrient cycling.
Biodiverse ecosystems are generally more resilient and can better withstand or recover from environmental changes.
For example, in a forest, many plant and animal species form food webs; insects pollinate plants, while decomposers recycle nutrients.
written.followUp: Explain how biodiversity supports food webs and nutrient cycling in a natural ecosystem.

rubric.why: Biodiversity helps keep ecosystems balanced and stable.
rubric.description: States that biodiversity supports ecosystem balance or stability.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that biodiversity helps maintain ecosystem balance or stability.

rubric.why: Different species are connected through feeding relationships.
rubric.description: Explains that species form food chains or food webs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning food chains or food webs.

rubric.why: Organisms contribute to recycling nutrients within ecosystems.
rubric.description: Links biodiversity with nutrient recycling.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that biodiversity supports nutrient cycling or nutrient recycling.

rubric.why: A biodiverse ecosystem is better able to withstand or recover from environmental changes.
rubric.description: States that biodiversity increases ecosystem resilience.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that biodiversity helps an ecosystem withstand or recover from changes.

rubric.why: A specific example illustrates biodiversity's importance in a natural ecosystem.
rubric.description: Gives a relevant ecosystem example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example linking forest species to pollination, food webs, or nutrient recycling.

written.text: State how the light intensity, concentration of carbondioxide and temperature affect the rate of photosynthesis?
modelAnswer: Increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis because light supplies the energy for the process; the rate levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate because carbon dioxide is a raw material; the rate also levels off when another factor becomes limiting.
Increasing temperature raises the rate up to an optimum because photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes.
Above the optimum temperature, the rate decreases as the enzymes lose their proper functioning.
written.followUp: Explain how increasing light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration affects photosynthesis, including the effect of a limiting factor.

rubric.why: Light supplies energy for photosynthesis, and greater intensity raises the rate up to a limit.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of light intensity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, so increasing its concentration raises the rate up to a limit.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of carbon dioxide concentration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, so temperature affects its rate.
rubric.description: Relates temperature to enzyme-controlled photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking temperature's effect on photosynthesis to enzymes.

rubric.why: Temperature has an optimum, and other factors can limit the rate; the rate does not increase indefinitely.
rubric.description: States the temperature limit or limiting-factor effect.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the rate decreases above the optimum temperature or levels off when another factor becomes limiting.

written.text: Explain (with the help of diagram) what would happen when plant and animal cells are placed in a hypertonic solution?
modelAnswer: In a hypertonic solution, water leaves both plant and animal cells by osmosis.
The animal cell shrinks (crenates) because it has no cell wall to resist the loss of water.
In the plant cell, the protoplast loses water and contracts away from the cell wall; this is called plasmolysis.
The rigid cell wall remains in place and helps retain the plant cell's outer shape.
Diagram construction: draw an animal-cell circle 2 cm in diameter and a smaller, crenated outline inside it; label it “animal cell in hypertonic solution.”
Draw a plant-cell rectangle 4 cm long × 2.5 cm high; draw a smaller protoplast, about 2.5 cm × 1.2 cm, separated from the wall; label “cell wall,” “plasmolysed protoplast,” and “hypertonic solution.”
Draw at least two arrows pointing out of each cell and label them “water.”
written.followUp: Explain what happens to a plant cell and an animal cell when they are placed in a hypotonic solution.

rubric.why: Water moves out of both cells by osmosis when they are placed in a hypertonic solution.
rubric.description: States the direction and process of water movement.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that water leaves both cells by osmosis.

rubric.why: The animal cell loses water and shrinks because it has no cell wall.
rubric.description: Describes the effect on the animal cell.

modelAnswer: The incubation period is the time between the entry of a pathogen into the body and the appearance of disease symptoms.
written.followUp: What is the incubation period, and when does it end?

rubric.why: Identifies the interval and its starting point.
rubric.description: It is a time interval beginning when a pathogen enters the body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is a time interval beginning with the pathogen’s entry.

rubric.why: Identifies the event that ends the period.
rubric.description: The incubation period ends when disease symptoms appear.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning the appearance of symptoms.

written.text: Write any four characteristics of Hypothesis.
modelAnswer: A hypothesis is a tentative explanation based on observations.
It should be logical and testable.
It can be accepted or rejected after testing.
It should be supported by evidence.
written.followUp: State four characteristics of a good hypothesis.

rubric.why: A hypothesis must be a reasoned, provisional explanation that can be checked.
rubric.description: Gives any two valid characteristics, such as testable, tentative, logical, or based on observations.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any two distinct valid characteristics.

rubric.why: Rewards further correct characteristics from the requested four.
rubric.description: Gives two further valid characteristics of a hypothesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two further distinct characteristics; do not credit a characteristic already counted.

written.text: How does theory become law? Give one example of law.
modelAnswer: In the textbook’s simplified account, a theory that is repeatedly tested and supported by evidence is stated as a scientific law.
An example is Mendel’s law of segregation.
written.followUp: How does a scientific theory become a law? Give one example of a scientific law.

rubric.why: Explains that repeated testing and supporting evidence establish the statement.
rubric.description: A theory that is repeatedly tested and supported by evidence is stated as a scientific law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning repeated testing and support by evidence.

rubric.why: Gives a valid example of a scientific law.
rubric.description: One example is Mendel’s law of segregation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming Mendel’s law of segregation.

written.text: What will happen when lysosome fuses with vacuole?
modelAnswer: The lysosome releases its digestive enzymes into the vacuole.
These enzymes digest the vacuole’s contents, resulting in intracellular digestion.
written.followUp: What happens to food in a vacuole after a lysosome fuses with it?

rubric.why: States what the lysosome contributes to the vacuole.
rubric.description: The lysosome releases digestive enzymes into the vacuole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that digestive enzymes enter or are released into the vacuole.

rubric.why: States the result of the fusion.
rubric.description: The enzymes digest the vacuole’s contents, carrying out intracellular digestion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the vacuole’s contents are digested.

written.text: How are "Taxonomy" and "Systematics" related?
modelAnswer: Taxonomy deals with the identification, naming, and classification of organisms.
It is a part of systematics, which also studies relationships among organisms, including their evolutionary relationships.
written.followUp: What is taxonomy, and how is it related to systematics?

rubric.why: Identifies the main activities of taxonomy.
rubric.description: Taxonomy deals with identification, naming, and classification of organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a relevant taxonomic activity.

rubric.why: Explains the broader scope of systematics and its relation to taxonomy.
rubric.description: Taxonomy is part of systematics; systematics also considers relationships among organisms, including evolutionary relationships.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the relationship or the broader scope of systematics.

written.text: Why we use criteria of interbreeding to define species of unicellular organism?
modelAnswer: The interbreeding criterion is not suitable for most unicellular organisms because they reproduce asexually and do not interbreed.
They are therefore grouped into species by similarities in their characteristics.
written.followUp: Why is the ability to produce fertile offspring used to distinguish species of sexually reproducing organisms?

rubric.why: Shows why interbreeding is not a suitable criterion for most unicellular organisms.
rubric.description: Most unicellular organisms reproduce asexually and do not interbreed.
rubric.how: Award for stating that they reproduce asexually or do not interbreed.

rubric.why: Identifies the basis used to group these organisms into species.
rubric.description: They are grouped into species by similarities in their characteristics.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning similarities in their characteristics.

written.text: What are the contribution of Carolous Linnaeus in the field of Classification?
modelAnswer: Carolus Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature, in which each organism is given a two-word scientific name.
He classified organisms into two kingdoms: Plantae and Animalia.
written.followUp: State two contributions of Carolus Linnaeus to the classification of organisms.

rubric.why: Binomial nomenclature is a major contribution associated with Linnaeus.
rubric.description: Introduced the system of binomial nomenclature for naming organisms.
rubric.how: Award for naming the system or describing its two-word naming method.

rubric.why: Linnaeus also arranged organisms into broad kingdoms.
rubric.description: Classified organisms into the kingdoms Plantae and Animalia.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the two kingdoms or stating that he classified plants and animals.

written.text: Write the names of four phases of Karyokinesis.
modelAnswer: The four phases of karyokinesis, in order, are prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
written.followUp: Name the four phases of mitosis in their correct order.

rubric.why: These are the four phases of karyokinesis in the correct order.
rubric.description: Names all four phases in order.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for all four correct in order; 1 mark for two or three correct phases or a minor ordering error.

written.text: Define the light dependent reaction.
modelAnswer: The light-dependent reaction is the stage of photosynthesis in which chlorophyll absorbs light energy and converts it into chemical energy in ATP and NADPH.
Water is split, releasing oxygen.
written.followUp: What are the main products of the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: The reaction converts light energy into chemical energy carriers.
rubric.description: States that light energy is converted into chemical energy, such as ATP and NADPH.
rubric.how: Award for the energy conversion or for naming ATP and NADPH.

rubric.why: Photolysis of water and oxygen release are key events in this reaction.
rubric.description: States that water is split and oxygen is released.
rubric.how: Award for mentioning water splitting and oxygen release.

written.text: Write the role of active site in enzyme.
modelAnswer: The active site is the part of an enzyme where a specific substrate binds because their shapes are complementary.
This binding forms an enzyme-substrate complex, allowing the enzyme to catalyse the reaction.
written.followUp: How does an enzyme-substrate complex form?

rubric.why: The substrate binds at the enzyme's active site.
rubric.description: The active site binds a specific substrate because their shapes are complementary.
rubric.how: Award for describing substrate binding at the active site or its specificity.

rubric.why: Binding at the active site enables the enzyme to catalyse the reaction.
rubric.description: Substrate binding forms an enzyme-substrate complex and allows catalysis.
rubric.how: Award for naming the complex or describing the catalytic role.

written.text: What is the function of arteries in human body? Write any two functions.
modelAnswer: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the body organs.
They usually carry oxygenated blood and have thick, elastic walls to withstand the high pressure of blood flow (the pulmonary artery is an exception).
written.followUp: What is the function of veins? Give two points.

rubric.why: The direction of blood flow is the main function of arteries.
rubric.description: Arteries carry blood away from the heart to body organs.
rubric.how: Award for stating that blood flows away from the heart.

rubric.why: These are characteristic functions or features that support arterial transport.
rubric.description: Usually carry oxygenated blood and withstand blood pressure with thick, elastic walls.
rubric.how: Award for one correct additional function or characteristic; allow mention that the pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood.

written.text: How would you explain that transpiration is harmful for plants?
modelAnswer: Transpiration is harmful when it is excessive because the plant loses water faster than it can absorb it.
The plant may wilt, its growth may be reduced, and it may eventually die.
written.followUp: Explain one way that excessive transpiration can damage a plant.

rubric.why: Identifies the harmful water loss caused by excessive transpiration.
rubric.description: The plant loses water faster than it can absorb it.
rubric.how: Award for stating that excessive transpiration causes water loss.

rubric.why: Names a consequence of excessive water loss.
rubric.description: Water loss may cause wilting, reduced growth or death.
rubric.how: Award for giving one valid consequence.

written.text: Write note on Molecular level of organization.
modelAnswer: At the molecular level, atoms combine to form molecules, which are the building materials of cell structures and organelles.
Molecules in organisms include organic molecules such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids.
Inorganic substances such as water, minerals and carbon dioxide are also present at this level.
written.followUp: Describe the cellular level of organization and give two examples of cell structures.

rubric.why: Molecules are formed from atoms at this level of organization.
rubric.description: Atoms combine to form molecules.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that molecules consist of atoms or are formed when atoms combine.

rubric.why: Molecules contribute to the structures that make up cells.
rubric.description: Molecules are the building materials of cell structures and organelles.
rubric.how: Award for linking molecules to cell structures, organelles or cells.

rubric.why: Organic biomolecules are important examples at the molecular level.
rubric.description: Gives examples of organic molecules found in organisms.
rubric.how: Award for suitable examples such as carbohydrates, proteins, lipids or nucleic acids.

rubric.why: Inorganic substances are also part of the molecular level.
rubric.description: Identifies examples of inorganic molecules or substances in organisms.
rubric.how: Award for a suitable example such as water, minerals or carbon dioxide.

written.text: Explain white blood cells.
modelAnswer: White blood cells, also called leucocytes, protect the body against pathogens and disease.
They can move out of blood vessels and engulf pathogens by phagocytosis.
Some white blood cells, such as lymphocytes, produce antibodies that help destroy pathogens.
White blood cells have a nucleus and do not contain haemoglobin.
written.followUp: Describe the structure and function of red blood cells.

rubric.why: White blood cells protect the body from pathogens.
rubric.description: State their protective role against pathogens.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking protection of the body to pathogens.

rubric.why: Phagocytosis is one way white blood cells destroy pathogens.
rubric.description: Explain that white blood cells engulf pathogens by phagocytosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing engulfment by phagocytosis.

rubric.why: Lymphocytes produce antibodies that help fight pathogens.
rubric.description: State that some white blood cells produce antibodies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying lymphocytes and antibody production.

rubric.why: White blood cells have a nucleus and can move out of blood vessels to reach affected tissues.
rubric.description: Give a structural feature and explain how white blood cells reach tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that they have a nucleus and 1 mark for stating that they can move out of blood vessels.

written.text: Explain macromolecules with two examples.
modelAnswer: Macromolecules are large molecules, often formed by joining many smaller molecules.
Examples include proteins and carbohydrates.
written.followUp: Define polymers and give two examples of biological polymers.

rubric.why: Macromolecules are large molecules, often made by joining smaller molecules.
rubric.description: Define macromolecules by their size and the smaller units from which they may be formed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing macromolecules as large molecules formed from smaller molecules.

rubric.why: Proteins and carbohydrates are examples of macromolecules.
rubric.description: Give two examples of macromolecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming any two valid examples.

written.text: What is population level? Give an example.
modelAnswer: Population level is a group of individuals of the same species living in a particular area at a particular time.
For example, all the frogs of one species living in a pond form a population.
written.followUp: Define community level and give an example.

rubric.why: A population consists of members of the same species living in a particular area.
rubric.description: Define population level using same species and area.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both elements of the definition.

rubric.why: A suitable example names a population of one species in a particular place.
rubric.description: Give a valid example of a population.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example such as frogs of the same species in a pond.

written.text: What is quina quina plant? Explain.
modelAnswer: Quina quina is the cinchona plant, whose bark contains the medicinal substance quinine.
Quinine is used to treat malaria.
written.followUp: Name the medicinal substance obtained from cinchona bark and state its use.

rubric.why: Quina quina is the common name used for the cinchona plant.
rubric.description: Identify quina quina as the cinchona plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the plant as cinchona/quina quina.

rubric.why: Cinchona bark provides quinine, a medicine used to treat malaria.
rubric.description: State that the plant yields quinine, used against malaria.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for quinine and its use in treating malaria.

written.text: What is the difference between law and principle?
modelAnswer: A law is a concise statement that describes a natural phenomenon.
A principle is a general rule based on scientific observations and experiments.
written.followUp: Differentiate between a scientific theory and a scientific law.

rubric.why: A law describes a natural phenomenon in a concise form.
rubric.description: Defines a law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a law is a concise statement describing a natural phenomenon.

rubric.why: A principle is a general rule supported by scientific observations or experiments.
rubric.description: Defines a principle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying a principle as a general rule based on scientific observations or experiments.

written.text: What is the difference between thylakoid and stroma?
modelAnswer: Thylakoids are flattened membrane sacs containing chlorophyll; they are arranged in stacks called grana.
The stroma is the fluid matrix of the chloroplast, containing enzymes, in which the grana are embedded.
written.followUp: Differentiate between grana and stroma in a chloroplast.

rubric.why: Thylakoids are flattened membrane sacs that contain chlorophyll.
rubric.description: Describes thylakoids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying thylakoids as flattened sacs or chlorophyll-containing structures.

rubric.why: The stroma is the chloroplast’s fluid matrix and contains enzymes.
rubric.description: Describes the stroma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the stroma as the fluid matrix or noting that it contains enzymes.

written.text: How can you differentiate between transmission electron microscope and scanning electron microscope?
modelAnswer: A transmission electron microscope (TEM) passes electrons through a thin specimen and shows its internal details.
A scanning electron microscope (SEM) scans the specimen’s surface and shows its surface details, usually as a three-dimensional image.
written.followUp: How does a light microscope differ from an electron microscope?

rubric.why: A TEM passes electrons through a thin specimen to reveal internal details.
rubric.description: Explains how a TEM forms an image.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that electrons pass through a thin specimen and show its internal structure.

rubric.why: An SEM scans the specimen’s surface to show its surface structure.
rubric.description: Explains how an SEM forms an image.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an SEM scans the specimen’s surface.

written.text: What are the defects of two - Kingdom classification system?
modelAnswer: The two-kingdom system does not distinguish between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
It grouped fungi with plants, although fungi lack chlorophyll.
written.followUp: State two differences between the five-kingdom and two-kingdom classification systems.

rubric.why: The two-kingdom system does not separate prokaryotes from eukaryotes.
rubric.description: Gives one defect of the system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it does not distinguish prokaryotic organisms from eukaryotic organisms.

rubric.why: Fungi were grouped with plants despite lacking chlorophyll and not making their own food like plants.
rubric.description: Gives another defect of the system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that fungi were classified with plants even though they lack chlorophyll.

written.text: Mule is not classified into species. Why?
modelAnswer: A mule is a hybrid offspring of a horse and a donkey.
Mules are generally sterile and cannot reproduce; therefore, they do not form a species.
written.followUp: Why are mules generally unable to produce offspring?

rubric.why: A mule is a hybrid produced by a horse and a donkey.
rubric.description: Identifies the mule as a hybrid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a mule is a horse–donkey hybrid.

rubric.why: Mules are generally sterile and cannot produce offspring, so they cannot form a reproducing species.
rubric.description: Explains why a mule is not classified as a species.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking its sterility or inability to reproduce to species classification.

written.text: Write down the functions of cell plate (Phragmoplast).
modelAnswer: The phragmoplast guides the formation of the cell plate between the daughter nuclei.
The cell plate grows outwards and develops into a new cell wall, separating the two daughter cells.
written.followUp: Describe how a cell plate forms during cytokinesis in a plant cell.

rubric.why: The phragmoplast guides the formation of the cell plate between the daughter nuclei.
rubric.description: States the role or location of the cell plate during cytokinesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the phragmoplast guides cell-plate formation or that the plate forms between the daughter nuclei.

rubric.why: The cell plate develops into a new cell wall that separates the daughter cells.
rubric.description: States the outcome of cell-plate formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the cell plate forms a new wall or separates the daughter cells.

written.text: Write the significance of Mitosis in cell replacement.
modelAnswer: Mitosis replaces worn-out, damaged or dead cells with new cells.
The daughter cells have the same chromosome number as the parent cell, maintaining the organism's tissues.
written.followUp: State two ways in which mitosis is important for an organism's growth and repair.

rubric.why: Mitosis produces new cells to replace worn-out, damaged or dead cells.
rubric.description: States that mitosis replaces cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning replacement of worn-out, damaged or dead cells.

rubric.why: Mitosis produces daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell, supporting continued cell replacement.
rubric.description: States the result of replacement by mitosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that mitosis maintains chromosome number or produces genetically identical daughter cells.

written.text: Define photosynthesis and write the equation of photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants use light energy, in the presence of chlorophyll, to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water, releasing oxygen.
6CO₂ + 6H₂O —(light, chlorophyll)→ C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
written.followUp: Define respiration and write its balanced equation.

rubric.why: The definition should identify photosynthesis as the light-driven process by which plants make food.
rubric.description: Defines photosynthesis as the process by which green plants use light energy to make glucose.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the essential idea that green plants use light energy to make glucose. Accept equivalent wording that includes chlorophyll.

rubric.why: The equation must show the reactants and products in the correct balanced proportions.
rubric.description: Writes the balanced equation for photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the balanced equation, with carbon dioxide and water as reactants and glucose and oxygen as products.

written.text: Define light reaction of photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: The light reaction is the light-dependent stage of photosynthesis in which chlorophyll absorbs light energy and converts it into chemical energy stored in ATP and NADPH.
Water is split (photolysis), releasing oxygen.
written.followUp: What is the dark reaction of photosynthesis?

rubric.why: The light reaction depends on light captured by chlorophyll and converts it into chemical energy.
rubric.description: States that the reaction occurs in light and that chlorophyll absorbs light energy, which is converted into chemical energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking light and chlorophyll with the conversion of light energy to chemical energy.

rubric.why: Splitting water supplies products used in photosynthesis and releases oxygen.
rubric.description: Mentions splitting of water and release of oxygen, or the formation of ATP and NADPH in the light reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either the water-splitting and oxygen-release point or the formation of ATP and NADPH.

written.text: Differentiate between the intracellular and extra cellular enzymes.
modelAnswer: Intracellular enzymes are produced and act inside the cells in which they are made.
Extracellular enzymes are produced by cells and secreted to act outside those cells.
written.followUp: Give one example each of an intracellular and an extracellular enzyme.

rubric.why: The key distinction is where an intracellular enzyme acts.
rubric.description: States that intracellular enzymes act inside the cells in which they are produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying their site of action as inside the cell.

rubric.why: Extracellular enzymes are released to act outside the cells that produce them.
rubric.description: States that extracellular enzymes are secreted and act outside the cells in which they are produced.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying secretion or action outside the cell.

written.text: Which model of enzyme action mechanism is suitable. State it.
modelAnswer: The induced-fit model is the suitable model of enzyme action.
The enzyme's active site is flexible; when a substrate binds, the active site changes shape to fit it and forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
written.followUp: Describe the lock-and-key model of enzyme action.

rubric.why: The suitable model is identified by name.
rubric.description: Names the induced-fit model of enzyme action.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming the induced-fit model.

rubric.why: The model explains substrate binding through a flexible active site that changes shape to fit the substrate.
rubric.description: Explains that the active site changes shape when the substrate binds, forming an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the active-site shape change and fit with the substrate.

written.text: Draw labeled diagram of stomach.
modelAnswer: Draw a curved, J-shaped sac with a rounded upper part (fundus), a central body and a narrower lower end.
Draw the oesophagus entering at the upper end and the duodenum leaving the lower end.
Label the fundus, body, oesophagus, pyloric sphincter and duodenum.
written.followUp: Draw and label the small intestine.

rubric.why: A recognizable stomach outline with its main regions is needed for a labeled biological diagram.

rubric.why: The entry and exit connections identify the stomach and its orientation.
rubric.description: Labels the oesophagus entry and the pyloric outlet leading to the duodenum; accept the cardiac sphincter as an entry label.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct entry and outlet labels, including the duodenum.

written.text: What is meant by vascular system?
modelAnswer: The vascular system is the system of conducting tissues that transports materials throughout a plant.
It consists of xylem and phloem.
written.followUp: Name the two vascular tissues in plants and state what each transports.

rubric.why: The plant vascular system consists of its conducting tissues, xylem and phloem.
rubric.description: Identifies xylem and phloem as the vascular tissues.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both xylem and phloem.

rubric.why: The vascular system conducts materials through the plant.
rubric.description: Defines the vascular system as the system that transports materials throughout a plant.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it conducts or transports substances through the plant.

written.text: Write any four professions which can be adopted after biological studies.
modelAnswer: Doctor or physician.
Pharmacist.
Agriculturist.
Biologist or biological researcher.
written.followUp: List four occupations related to the study of biology.

rubric.why: Medicine is a profession that can be pursued after biological studies.
rubric.description: Names one biology-related profession in medicine.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid medical profession, such as doctor, physician or surgeon.

rubric.why: Pharmacy is a profession that uses biological knowledge.
rubric.description: Names pharmacy or a pharmacist as a profession.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for pharmacist or pharmacy.

rubric.why: Agriculture-related careers apply biological knowledge to crops and farming.
rubric.description: Names one profession related to agriculture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid agriculture-related profession.

written.text: What do you know about National conservation strategy for biodiversity? Explain it.

written.text: How would you distinguish between aerobic and anaerobic respiration? Explain anaerobic respiration.
modelAnswer: Aerobic respiration requires oxygen, whereas anaerobic respiration takes place without oxygen.

rubric.why: Describes the defining property and function of muscle tissue.

written.text: Define the highest level in the levels of organization of organisms.
modelAnswer: The biosphere is the highest level in the levels of organization of organisms.

written.text: Why viruses are excluded from five kingdom classification system?
modelAnswer: Viruses are excluded from the five-kingdom classification because they are acellular and lack cellular structure.

written.text: How are oxidation-reduction reactions involved in energy transfer in living organism?

written.text: How saturation of active sites take place?

written.text: Differentiate between source & sink and how sink is converted into source.
modelAnswer: A source is a plant part, such as a mature leaf, that produces and exports sugars; a sink is a part that uses or stores sugars, such as a growing region or tuber.

When ATP is hydrolysed, it breaks down into ADP and phosphate and releases usable energy.
This energy is transferred to cellular processes that require energy.
ATP is therefore called the cell's energy currency.

modelAnswer: Vitamin A is essential for normal vision and maintaining healthy epithelial tissues; its deficiency can cause night blindness.

written.text: What is a Habitat?
modelAnswer: A habitat is the natural place or environment in which an organism lives.

written.text: Differentiate between Biomathematics and Bioeconomics.
modelAnswer: Biomathematics applies mathematical methods and models to solve problems in biology.
Bioeconomics applies economic principles to the study and management of biological resources.

written.text: How Horticulture is beneficial to man?
modelAnswer: Horticulture provides people with fruits and vegetables for food.

written.text: Which Two tools Darwin used to manipulate his theory of evolution?
modelAnswer: Darwin used natural selection as a tool to explain evolution.

written.text: Give four characteristics of good hypothesis.
modelAnswer: A good hypothesis is clear and simple.
It is testable and can be falsified.
It is based on observations.
It can make predictions.

rubric.why: A good hypothesis has several qualities that make it useful for scientific investigation.
rubric.description: Gives four valid characteristics of a good hypothesis.
rubric.how: Award 0.5 mark for each distinct valid characteristic, up to 2 marks. Examples include clear, simple, testable, falsifiable, based on observations, and predictive.

written.text: Compare the work of Camillo Golgi and Christian Rene DeDuve.
modelAnswer: Camillo Golgi discovered the Golgi apparatus.
Christian de Duve discovered lysosomes.

rubric.why: Golgi's work led to the identification of the Golgi apparatus.
rubric.description: Identifies the structure discovered by Camillo Golgi.

written.text: Define the Cell Cycle?
modelAnswer: The cell cycle is the ordered series of events that takes place in a cell.
It leads to the cell's division into two daughter cells.
written.followUp: Name the main stages of the cell cycle.

rubric.why: The cell cycle is defined as an ordered series of events in a cell.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing it as an ordered series or sequence of cellular events.

rubric.why: The defining sequence culminates in cell division and formation of daughter cells.
rubric.description: States that the sequence leads to cell division, producing two daughter cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the outcome of the cycle as division into two daughter cells.

written.text: Why three kingdom system was needed?
modelAnswer: The two-kingdom system was inadequate because many organisms, especially unicellular organisms, could not be placed properly in either Plantae or Animalia.
Therefore, Haeckel proposed a third kingdom, Protista, for these organisms.
written.followUp: Which organisms were placed in kingdom Protista in Haeckel’s three-kingdom system?

rubric.why: The two-kingdom system did not provide a suitable place for some organisms.
rubric.description: States that the two-kingdom system was inadequate for classifying some organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the limitation of the two-kingdom system.

rubric.why: Protista provided a separate group for organisms that did not fit properly in Plantae or Animalia.
rubric.description: States that Haeckel added Protista as a third kingdom for these organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming Protista and its role as the third kingdom.

written.text: Write the short Note on Houbara bustard.
modelAnswer: The Houbara bustard is a migratory bird that visits Pakistan in winter, travelling from Central Asia.
It is threatened by hunting and therefore needs protection.
written.followUp: Why is the Houbara bustard considered a threatened migratory bird?

written.text: Write the difference between FADH and NADH
modelAnswer: NADH and FADH₂ are reduced coenzymes that carry hydrogen/electrons to the electron transport chain.

written.text: Define Glycolysis? Write its end product.
modelAnswer: Glycolysis is the breakdown of one glucose molecule into two molecules of pyruvic acid in the cytoplasm.
Its end product is two molecules of pyruvic acid (pyruvate).
written.followUp: Define glycolysis and state its end product.

written.text: How does pH affect enzyme activity.
modelAnswer: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it has maximum activity.
A pH above or below the optimum can change the enzyme’s structure and active site, so its activity decreases; extreme pH may denature it.
written.followUp: Explain how temperature affects enzyme activity.

rubric.why: Identifies the pH at which an enzyme works best.
rubric.description: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it has maximum activity.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a structural or active-site change, or denaturation, that reduces activity.

written.text: What do you mean by De-naturation of enzyme.
modelAnswer: Denaturation is a change in an enzyme’s structure, often caused by high temperature or extreme pH.
The active site changes shape, so the substrate cannot bind properly and the enzyme loses its activity.
written.followUp: What is enzyme denaturation, and what happens to the enzyme’s active site?

rubric.why: Defines denaturation as a change in enzyme structure and identifies a possible cause.
rubric.description: Denaturation is a change in an enzyme’s structure, often caused by high temperature or extreme pH.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the structural change or a cause of denaturation.

rubric.why: States the effect of denaturation on enzyme function.
rubric.description: The changed active site prevents proper substrate binding, so the enzyme loses its activity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the active site changes or that the enzyme loses function.

written.text: What are “arteries” and “veins”?
modelAnswer: Arteries are blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart.
Veins are blood vessels that carry blood towards the heart.
written.followUp: State the direction in which arteries and veins carry blood.

rubric.why: Identifies the direction of blood flow in arteries.

written.text: What role does the pericardial fluid play?
modelAnswer: Pericardial fluid lies between the membranes surrounding the heart.
It lubricates the surfaces, reduces friction and allows the heart to beat smoothly.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that it allows smooth heart movement during beating.

written.text: Write a comprehensive note on cellular organizations by explaining various types of organisms.
modelAnswer: In unicellular organisms, a single cell performs all the functions needed for life; for example, Amoeba.
In colonial organisms, similar cells live together in a group or colony; Volvox is an example.
Multicellular organisms consist of many cells, often specialized for different functions; humans are an example.
Specialized cells work together through division of labour and may form tissues and organs.
written.followUp: Describe unicellular, colonial and multicellular organisms, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Describes unicellular organization or gives a suitable example.

rubric.why: Describes colonial organization or gives a suitable example.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the defining feature of multicellular organisms or a suitable example.

rubric.description: Specialized cells work together through division of labour and may form tissues and organs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating division of labour or describing organization into tissues and organs.

written.text: Explain different factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Light: bright light usually opens stomata and increases transpiration; darkness generally lowers it.
Temperature: higher temperature increases evaporation from leaf surfaces and usually raises the rate of transpiration.
Humidity: low humidity increases transpiration, while high humidity reduces the difference in water-vapour concentration and lowers it.
Wind: moving air removes moist air around the leaf, usually increasing transpiration.
Soil water: adequate water supply supports transpiration; water shortage may cause stomata to close and reduce it.
Leaf features: larger leaf area and more stomata generally increase transpiration, while a thick waxy cuticle reduces water loss.
written.followUp: Explain how humidity, wind and the number of stomata affect the rate of transpiration.

rubric.why: Explains the effects of light and temperature on transpiration.
rubric.description: Bright light usually opens stomata and increases transpiration; higher temperature increases evaporation and usually raises the rate.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for correctly explaining both light and temperature effects.

rubric.why: Explains how humidity affects water-vapour loss.
rubric.description: Low humidity increases transpiration, whereas high humidity reduces it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly explaining the effect of humidity.

rubric.why: Explains how wind affects the air around the leaf.
rubric.description: Wind removes moist air around the leaf and usually increases transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly explaining the effect of wind.

rubric.why: Identifies a leaf feature or water-supply factor that affects transpiration.
rubric.description: Larger leaf area or more stomata generally increases transpiration; a thick waxy cuticle reduces it. Adequate soil water supports transpiration, while water shortage may cause stomata to close.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct leaf-structure or water-availability factor and its effect.

written.text: Write the summary events of light reactions of Photosynthesis.
modelAnswer: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy in the photosystems.
Light energy splits water molecules into electrons, hydrogen ions and oxygen; this process is called photolysis.
Electrons pass along an electron transport chain, and their energy is used to form ATP by photophosphorylation.
NADP accepts electrons and hydrogen ions and is reduced to NADPH.
Oxygen is released as a by-product; ATP and NADPH are used in the light-independent reactions.
written.followUp: List the main products of the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis and state how each is formed.

rubric.why: Recognizes the capture of light energy that starts the reactions.
rubric.description: Chlorophyll absorbs light energy.
rubric.how: Award for naming chlorophyll or photosystems and the absorption of light.

rubric.why: Identifies the source of electrons and hydrogen ions.
rubric.description: Light energy splits water into electrons, hydrogen ions and oxygen.
rubric.how: Award for stating that water is split by light.

rubric.why: Identifies ATP formation in the light reactions.
rubric.description: Electron transport drives ATP formation by photophosphorylation.
rubric.how: Award for linking ATP production with photophosphorylation or electron transport.

rubric.why: Identifies the reduced electron carrier produced.
rubric.description: NADP accepts electrons and hydrogen to form NADPH.
rubric.how: Award for stating that NADP is reduced to NADPH.

rubric.why: Identifies oxygen as a product of water splitting.
rubric.description: Oxygen is released as a by-product of photolysis.
rubric.how: Award for naming oxygen and indicating that it is released.

written.text: Proteins and Lipids are the best source of energy. Interpret.
modelAnswer: When food molecules are oxidized in cells, their chemical energy is released.
One gram of lipid yields about 9 kcal, while one gram of protein yields about 4 kcal.
One gram of carbohydrate also yields about 4 kcal.
Therefore, lipids are the most concentrated energy source per gram; the statement is not fully correct if it calls proteins the best energy source as well.
Proteins can be used for energy, but their main roles are growth and repair, and they are not normally the body's preferred fuel.
written.followUp: Compare the energy released by the oxidation of one gram of carbohydrates, proteins and lipids.

rubric.why: Gives the energy yield of lipids and identifies their high energy value.
rubric.description: Lipids yield about 9 kcal per gram, the greatest energy yield among these food groups.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the value and 1 mark for identifying lipids as the highest-yielding.

rubric.why: Gives the energy yield of proteins.
rubric.description: Proteins yield about 4 kcal per gram.
rubric.how: Award for the correct approximate value.

rubric.why: Provides the comparison needed to interpret the claim.
rubric.description: Carbohydrates also yield about 4 kcal per gram.
rubric.how: Award for the correct approximate value.

rubric.why: Clarifies the role of proteins rather than treating them as the body's preferred fuel.
rubric.description: Proteins are mainly used for growth and repair; they can provide energy, but are not normally the preferred energy source.
rubric.how: Award for stating the main structural role or that proteins are not the preferred fuel.
