written.text: What is the role of root hairs in absorption of water?
modelAnswer: Root hairs greatly increase the surface area of the root in contact with the soil.
Water enters the root hair cells from the soil by osmosis.
written.followUp: Explain how the structure of a root hair helps it absorb water from the soil.

rubric.why: Explains how root hairs increase the area available for absorption.
rubric.description: States that root hairs provide a large surface area for water absorption.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking root hairs with an increased absorptive surface area.

rubric.why: Identifies osmosis as the process by which water enters root hairs.
rubric.description: States that water moves from the soil into root hair cells by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying osmosis as the method of water uptake.

written.text: List the factors affecting the rate of transpiration.
modelAnswer: Factors affecting the rate of transpiration include light intensity, temperature, humidity, wind velocity and water availability.
Leaf area also affects the rate of transpiration.
written.followUp: Name four environmental factors that affect the rate of transpiration.

rubric.why: Assesses whether the student can name multiple factors influencing transpiration.
rubric.description: Names four relevant factors, such as light intensity, temperature, humidity, wind, water availability or leaf area.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for four valid factors; award 1 mark for two or three valid factors.

written.text: Why do stomata open and close? Illustrate this phenomenon.
modelAnswer: A stoma is surrounded by two guard cells.
In light, water enters the guard cells by osmosis; they become turgid and the stomatal pore opens.
In darkness, water leaves the guard cells; they become flaccid and the pore closes.
Illustration: Turgid guard cells → OPEN pore; flaccid guard cells → CLOSED pore.
written.followUp: Describe how water loss from leaves can affect a plant.

rubric.why: Identifies the structures controlling the stomatal opening.
rubric.description: Each stoma is surrounded by two guard cells.
rubric.how: Award for naming guard cells and the pore or stoma they surround.

rubric.why: Explains the change that leads to opening.
rubric.description: In light, water enters guard cells by osmosis.
rubric.how: Award for stating that light is associated with water entering the guard cells.

rubric.why: Connects guard-cell turgidity with the open pore.
rubric.description: The guard cells become turgid and the stomatal pore opens.
rubric.how: Award for correctly linking turgidity with opening.

rubric.why: Explains the change that leads to closing.
rubric.description: In darkness, water leaves the guard cells.
rubric.how: Award for stating that water leaves the guard cells, typically in darkness.

rubric.why: Completes the closing mechanism and illustrates the phenomenon.
rubric.description: The guard cells become flaccid and the pore closes; an illustration distinguishes open and closed stomata.
rubric.how: Award for linking flaccidity with closing, or for a clear labeled illustration showing open and closed stomata.

written.text: Write down any four steps to conserve biodiversity.
modelAnswer: Establish national parks and wildlife sanctuaries to protect habitats and species.
Enforce laws against hunting and poaching.
Plant trees and restore damaged habitats.
Conserve species in seed banks, botanical gardens, and zoos, and promote public awareness.
written.followUp: Write down four ways in which people can help conserve biodiversity.

rubric.why: Recognizes protection of habitats and wildlife.
rubric.description: Establish protected areas such as national parks or wildlife sanctuaries.
rubric.how: Award for any valid protected-area measure.

rubric.why: Recognizes the need to prevent killing or illegal trade of organisms.
rubric.description: Enforce laws against hunting and poaching.
rubric.how: Award for a measure that controls hunting, poaching, or wildlife trade.

rubric.why: Recognizes restoration or protection of habitats.
rubric.description: Plant trees and restore natural habitats.
rubric.how: Award for afforestation, reforestation, or another valid habitat-restoration measure.

rubric.why: Recognizes another valid conservation approach.
rubric.description: Use conservation facilities or educate the public about biodiversity.
rubric.how: Award for one additional valid measure, such as seed banks, botanical gardens, zoos, or public education.

written.text: What is the structure of a cell wall? Write down its importance.
modelAnswer: The cell wall is the rigid, non-living outer covering of a plant cell.
It is made mainly of cellulose and is freely permeable.
It gives the cell shape, support, and protection.
It helps prevent the cell from bursting when water enters.
written.followUp: Describe the structure and two functions of the cell membrane.

rubric.why: Describes the position and material of the plant cell wall.
rubric.description: The cell wall is a rigid, non-living outer covering made mainly of cellulose.
rubric.how: Award one mark for its outer, rigid, non-living nature and one for cellulose composition.

rubric.why: Identifies the cell wall's structural role.
rubric.description: It gives the cell support, protection, and shape.
rubric.how: Award for two of support, protection, or maintaining shape.

rubric.why: Identifies another important property or function.
rubric.description: It helps prevent the cell from bursting when water enters; it is freely permeable.
rubric.how: Award for preventing bursting or stating that the wall is freely permeable.

written.text: What do you know about the stomach in human body? Write down its structure and functions.
modelAnswer: The stomach is a muscular, J-shaped sac in the upper abdomen, between the oesophagus and small intestine.
Its inner lining contains gastric glands that secrete gastric juice, including hydrochloric acid, pepsin, and protective mucus.
The stomach temporarily stores food and churns it, mixing it with gastric juice.
Hydrochloric acid provides an acidic medium and helps kill microbes.
Pepsin begins protein digestion, and the partly digested food becomes semi-liquid chyme.
written.followUp: Describe the structure and functions of the small intestine.

rubric.why: Describes the stomach's form and general structure.
rubric.description: The stomach is a muscular, J-shaped sac.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the stomach as muscular and J-shaped or sac-like.

rubric.why: Locates the stomach in the digestive tract.
rubric.description: It lies between the oesophagus and the small intestine.
rubric.how: Award for correctly naming both connections.

rubric.why: Describes its secretory lining and digestive juices.
rubric.description: Its inner lining has gastric glands that secrete gastric juice, including hydrochloric acid, pepsin, and mucus.
rubric.how: Award for naming gastric glands and a relevant secretion or for naming two relevant components of gastric juice.

rubric.why: States a mechanical or storage function.
rubric.description: It temporarily stores food and churns it.
rubric.how: Award for storage or churning of food.

rubric.why: States a digestive function.
rubric.description: It begins protein digestion and mixes food into semi-liquid chyme.
rubric.how: Award for protein digestion or formation of chyme.

written.text: How can you define the term “unicellular organisms”? Give an example.
modelAnswer: A unicellular organism is an organism made up of a single cell that performs all the functions of life.
Example: Amoeba.
written.followUp: Define multicellular organisms and give one example.

rubric.why: States the defining feature of unicellular organisms.
rubric.description: A unicellular organism consists of a single cell that carries out all life functions.
rubric.how: Award for stating that it is made of one cell and that the cell performs life functions.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example.
rubric.description: Examples include Amoeba, bacteria, Paramecium, and yeast.
rubric.how: Award for any valid unicellular organism.

written.text: How does the Morphology differ from Anatomy?
modelAnswer: Morphology is the study of the external form and structure of an organism.
Anatomy is the study of the internal structure of an organism.
written.followUp: How does physiology differ from morphology?

rubric.why: Defines morphology as the study of external form.
rubric.description: Morphology deals with the external form and structure of organisms.
rubric.how: Award for describing morphology as the study of external form, structure, shape, or size.

rubric.why: Defines anatomy as the study of internal structure.
rubric.description: Anatomy deals with the internal structure of organisms.
rubric.how: Award for describing anatomy as the study of internal structure or internal parts.

written.text: Define organelle. Give an example of organelle.
modelAnswer: An organelle is a specialized structure within a cell that performs a specific function.
Example: Mitochondrion.
written.followUp: Define tissue and give an example of a tissue.

rubric.why: Explains what an organelle is and its role in a cell.
rubric.description: An organelle is a specialized structure within a cell that performs a particular function.
rubric.how: Award for identifying it as a specialized cell structure or part with a specific function.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of an organelle.
rubric.description: Examples include mitochondrion, nucleus, chloroplast, and ribosome.
rubric.how: Award for any valid cell organelle.

written.text: How does a theory become a law? Give an example of any biological law.
modelAnswer: A theory that is repeatedly tested and supported by evidence may be accepted as a scientific law.
Mendel’s law of segregation is an example of a biological law.
written.followUp: State one difference between a scientific theory and a scientific law, and give an example of a biological law.

rubric.why: Explains how a theory is accepted as a law in the textbook account.
rubric.description: A theory is repeatedly tested and supported by evidence before it is accepted as a law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking repeated testing or verification with acceptance as a law.

rubric.why: Gives an example of a biological law.
rubric.description: Names a biological law, such as Mendel’s law of segregation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

written.text: Write down a note on the services of Laveran regarding malaria.
modelAnswer: In 1880, Alphonse Laveran discovered the malaria parasite, Plasmodium.
He observed it in the blood of malaria patients.
written.followUp: Who discovered the malaria parasite, and where did he find it?

rubric.why: Identifies Laveran’s important discovery.
rubric.description: Laveran discovered that malaria is caused by a parasite.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Laveran discovered the malaria parasite.

rubric.why: States where the parasite was observed.
rubric.description: He observed the parasite in the blood of malaria patients.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the blood of malaria patients as the place of observation.

written.text: What is the importance of control in an experiment?
modelAnswer: A control provides a standard for comparison with the experimental group.
This helps show whether a change in the results is due to the variable being tested.
written.followUp: Why is a control group used when testing the effect of a variable?

rubric.why: Identifies the control’s role as a basis for comparison.
rubric.description: A control provides a standard for comparison with the experimental group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it provides a comparison or standard.

rubric.why: Explains how comparison helps assess the experimental factor.
rubric.description: It helps determine whether the observed effect is due to the variable being tested.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for connecting the comparison to judging the effect of the tested variable.

written.text: Why are the colours of petals in a flower different from those of leaves?
modelAnswer: Leaves are green because their cells contain chlorophyll in chloroplasts.
Petals contain other pigments, often in chromoplasts, which give them colours different from leaves.
written.followUp: What pigments give leaves their green colour and many petals their bright colours?

rubric.why: Identifies the pigment responsible for the colour of leaves.
rubric.description: Leaves are green because they contain chlorophyll in chloroplasts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying chlorophyll as the leaf pigment.

rubric.why: Explains why petals have colours different from leaves.
rubric.description: Petals contain other pigments, commonly in chromoplasts, which produce their colours.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying petal pigments or chromoplasts.

written.text: How is the cuboidal epithelium different from columnar epithelium?
modelAnswer: Cuboidal epithelial cells are cube-shaped, with their height and width approximately equal.
Columnar epithelial cells are tall and column-shaped, with their height greater than their width.
written.followUp: Compare the shape and usual location of cuboidal and columnar epithelial cells.

rubric.why: Identifies the characteristic shape of cuboidal epithelial cells.
rubric.description: Cuboidal epithelial cells are cube-shaped.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the cells as cube-shaped or cubical.

rubric.why: Distinguishes the shape of columnar epithelial cells from that of cuboidal cells.
rubric.description: Columnar epithelial cells are tall and column-shaped, with their height greater than their width.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the cells as tall or column-shaped, or stating that their height is greater than their width.

written.text: Describe the term biodiversity.
modelAnswer: Biodiversity is the variety of living organisms found in an area or on Earth.
It includes the diversity of species, such as plants, animals and microorganisms.
written.followUp: What is meant by species diversity?

rubric.why: Captures the central idea of biodiversity as variety.
rubric.description: Biodiversity means the variety of living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining it as variety among organisms.

rubric.why: Shows the range of organisms included in biodiversity.
rubric.description: It includes the diversity of species, such as plants, animals and microorganisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning species or examples of organism groups.

written.text: How did Margulis and Schwartz modify the five-kingdom classification of Robert Whittaker?
modelAnswer: Margulis and Schwartz modified Whittaker’s five-kingdom classification by dividing Monera into two kingdoms, making six kingdoms.
The two kingdoms were Archaebacteria and Eubacteria.
written.followUp: Into which two kingdoms was Monera divided in the six-kingdom classification?

rubric.why: States the main change made to Whittaker’s classification.
rubric.description: Margulis and Schwartz modified the five-kingdom system by dividing Monera into two kingdoms, producing a six-kingdom system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Monera was split and the system had six kingdoms.

rubric.why: Names the two kingdoms formed by the division.
rubric.description: The two kingdoms were Archaebacteria and Eubacteria.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both kingdoms.

written.text: Define viroids.
modelAnswer: Viroids are infectious agents made of a short, circular RNA molecule.
They have no protein coat and consist only of RNA.
written.followUp: How do viroids differ from viruses in their structure?

rubric.why: Identifies the basic structure of a viroid.
rubric.description: A viroid consists of a short, circular RNA molecule.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is made of circular RNA.

rubric.why: Distinguishes viroids from viruses by the absence of a protein coat.
rubric.description: Viroids have no protein coat and consist only of RNA.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that viroids lack a protein coat or consist only of RNA.

written.text: Differentiate between Mitosis and Binary Fission.
modelAnswer: Mitosis is cell division in eukaryotic cells; it involves division of the nucleus before the cell divides.
Binary fission is a simpler division in which a prokaryotic cell divides into two daughter cells.
written.followUp: State one difference between mitosis and meiosis.

rubric.why: Identifies the different kinds of cells in which these divisions typically occur.
rubric.description: Correctly contrasts the cells or organisms in which mitosis and binary fission occur.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that mitosis occurs in eukaryotic cells and binary fission typically occurs in prokaryotes.

rubric.why: States a distinguishing feature of the division process or its outcome.
rubric.description: Gives a correct difference in the process or outcome.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for noting that mitosis involves nuclear division followed by cell division, while binary fission divides one cell into two.

written.text: What are somatic cells?
modelAnswer: Somatic cells are the body cells other than the reproductive cells (gametes).
They are generally diploid, containing two sets of chromosomes.
written.followUp: What are germ cells?

rubric.why: Shows that somatic cells are the non-reproductive cells of the body.
rubric.description: Identifies somatic cells as body cells, rather than reproductive cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing them as body or non-reproductive cells.

rubric.why: Adds a common defining feature of somatic cells.
rubric.description: States that somatic cells generally contain two sets of chromosomes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as diploid.

written.text: Write down the names of two components of ATP molecule.
modelAnswer: ATP is made of adenine, ribose sugar and three phosphate groups.
Two of its components are adenine and ribose sugar.
written.followUp: Name the three types of subunits that make up an ATP molecule.

rubric.why: Identifies the nitrogenous base and sugar components of ATP.
rubric.description: Names adenine and ribose sugar.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both names.

rubric.why: Identifies the phosphate component of ATP.
rubric.description: Names the phosphate groups, including that there are three.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the phosphate groups.

written.text: Show the effect of temperature on the rate of enzyme action with the help of graph.
modelAnswer: Draw the horizontal axis as temperature (°C), from 0 to 60, using 10°C per division.
Draw the vertical axis as relative rate of enzyme action (%), from 0 to 100, using 10% per division.
Plot the representative points (temperature, relative rate): (0°C, 0%), (20°C, 50%), (37°C, 100%) and (60°C, 0%).
Join the points with a smooth curve that rises to a peak near 37°C and then falls sharply. Label the peak as the optimum temperature.
written.followUp: Draw a labelled graph showing how enzyme activity changes as substrate concentration increases.

rubric.why: The graph must identify the variables on both axes.
rubric.description: Labels the temperature and enzyme activity axes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly labelling the horizontal axis as temperature and the vertical axis as rate of enzyme action or activity.

rubric.why: Shows that enzyme activity rises to an optimum and then falls at higher temperatures.
rubric.description: Shows the characteristic rise to an optimum followed by a steep decline.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correctly shaped curve, with activity increasing to an optimum and then decreasing at high temperature.

written.text: What is meant by saturated active sites?
modelAnswer: Active sites are saturated when substrate molecules occupy all the available active sites of the enzymes.
The reaction is then at its maximum rate, so adding more substrate does not increase the rate.
written.followUp: What happens to the rate of an enzyme-controlled reaction when substrate concentration is increased after all active sites are occupied?

rubric.why: Defines saturation in terms of substrate occupying the enzyme active sites.
rubric.description: States that all enzyme active sites are occupied by substrate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this definition.

rubric.why: Explains the consequence of active-site saturation for reaction rate.
rubric.description: States that the reaction is at its maximum rate and further substrate does not increase it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the consequence.

written.text: Write down the names of two components of food used daily by humans in which weight of one gram of each food has the same amount of energy.
modelAnswer: Carbohydrates and proteins provide the same amount of energy per gram.
Each provides about 4 kilocalories (approximately 17 kilojoules) per gram.
written.followUp: Which two food components provide about 4 kilocalories of energy per gram each?

rubric.why: Carbohydrates provide approximately 4 kilocalories of energy per gram.
rubric.description: Names carbohydrates.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for carbohydrates.

rubric.why: Proteins provide approximately 4 kilocalories of energy per gram.
rubric.description: Names proteins.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for proteins.

written.text: What is meant by transpirational pull? Write down its importance also.
modelAnswer: Transpirational pull is the pulling force created in the xylem when water evaporates from the leaves during transpiration.
It helps draw water and dissolved minerals from the roots up through the xylem to the leaves; this upward movement is called the ascent of sap.
written.followUp: Explain how transpiration helps in the upward movement of water and minerals in a plant.

rubric.why: Identifies water evaporation from the leaves as the source of the pulling force.
rubric.description: Defines transpirational pull as the pulling force produced when water evaporates from leaves during transpiration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking water loss from leaves with a pulling force.

rubric.why: States the role of the pull in the upward movement of water and minerals.
rubric.description: Explains that it helps move water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots through the xylem to the leaves.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the pull helps in the upward transport of water and minerals, or that it causes the ascent of sap.

written.text: Why is the sound of lubb-dubb produced in the heart?
modelAnswer: The sound lubb is produced when the atrioventricular valves close as the ventricles begin to contract.
The sound dubb is produced when the semilunar valves close as the ventricles begin to relax.
written.followUp: What causes the first and second heart sounds?

rubric.why: The first heart sound is associated with closure of the atrioventricular valves.
rubric.description: Explains the cause of the lubb sound.
rubric.how: Award for linking lubb to closure of the atrioventricular (bicuspid and tricuspid) valves.

rubric.why: The second heart sound is associated with closure of the semilunar valves.
rubric.description: Explains the cause of the dubb sound.
rubric.how: Award for linking dubb to closure of the semilunar valves.

written.text: Write down cellular organization at molecular and cell level.
modelAnswer: At the molecular level, atoms combine to form molecules, and molecules can combine to form larger biological molecules.
These molecules form the structures of cell organelles.
At the cell level, organelles are organized within a cell and perform specific functions.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
written.followUp: Describe the tissue level and organ level of biological organization.

rubric.why: Atoms join together to form molecules.
rubric.description: Describes the formation of molecules at the molecular level.
rubric.how: Award for stating that atoms combine to form molecules.

rubric.why: Small molecules can join to form larger biological molecules.
rubric.description: Describes the formation of larger molecules.
rubric.how: Award for stating that molecules form larger molecules or macromolecules.

rubric.why: Molecules are organized into cell structures, including organelles.
rubric.description: Connects molecules with organelles.
rubric.how: Award for relating molecules to the formation or structure of organelles.

rubric.why: A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life, with organelles organized within it.
rubric.description: Describes the cell level of organization.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the cell as the basic unit of life or stating that organelles are organized within a cell.

written.text: Write down a note on transport of water in plants with the help of a diagram.
modelAnswer: Water in the soil enters root hairs by osmosis.
It moves through the root tissues and enters the xylem vessels.
Xylem transports water upwards through the roots and stem to the leaves.
Transpiration from the leaves creates a transpiration pull that helps draw water upwards.
Diagram: Soil water → root hair → root xylem → stem xylem ↑ → leaf xylem → leaf cells; water vapour exits through stomata.
written.followUp: Describe how food manufactured in leaves is transported through a plant.

rubric.why: Water enters the plant from the soil through root hairs by osmosis.
rubric.description: Explains water uptake by roots.
rubric.how: Award for identifying root hairs and osmosis as the route and process of water absorption.

rubric.why: Water passes through root tissues and enters the xylem.
rubric.description: Describes movement of water into root xylem.
rubric.how: Award for stating that water moves through the root to the xylem.

rubric.why: Xylem vessels conduct water from roots upwards through the stem.
rubric.description: Describes upward transport in xylem.
rubric.how: Award for identifying xylem as the upward water-conducting tissue.

rubric.why: Water loss from leaves creates a pull that helps draw water upwards.
rubric.description: Explains the role of transpiration pull.
rubric.how: Award for linking transpiration to the upward movement of water.

rubric.why: A labeled diagram should show the continuous route of water through the plant.
rubric.description: Provides a clear, labeled transport diagram.
rubric.how: Award for a diagram or clear arrow sequence showing the route from roots through xylem to leaves; accept labels for root, stem, leaf, and/or stomata.

written.text: What is an endangered species? Explain endangered species in Pakistan.
modelAnswer: An endangered species is a species whose numbers have fallen so much that it is at risk of extinction.
Examples of endangered species in Pakistan include the markhor, Indus river dolphin, snow leopard, and houbara bustard.
They are threatened by factors such as hunting and poaching, habitat loss, and pollution.
written.followUp: Define a vulnerable species and give one example from Pakistan.

rubric.why: An endangered species faces a high risk of extinction.
rubric.description: Defines an endangered species.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the species is in danger of extinction; give both marks for a clear definition including the risk of disappearing.

rubric.why: Pakistan has several endangered animal species.
rubric.description: Names a suitable endangered species found in Pakistan.
rubric.how: Award for one valid Pakistan example, such as markhor, Indus river dolphin, snow leopard, or houbara bustard.

rubric.why: Human activities and habitat changes threaten these species.
rubric.description: States a reason species are endangered in Pakistan.
rubric.how: Award for one relevant threat, such as hunting, poaching, habitat loss, or pollution.

written.text: What are limiting factors in photosynthesis? Explain.
modelAnswer: A limiting factor is a condition in short supply that restricts the rate of photosynthesis.
Light intensity affects the rate: as light intensity increases, the rate rises until another factor becomes limiting.
Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis; a low concentration limits the rate, while increasing it raises the rate up to a limit.
Temperature affects the enzymes involved in photosynthesis; low temperatures slow the reactions and very high temperatures can damage enzymes.
Water and chlorophyll are also necessary, and a shortage of either can limit photosynthesis.
written.followUp: Explain how light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration affect the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: A limiting factor is one that restricts the rate of photosynthesis when in short supply.
rubric.description: Defines a limiting factor.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that the factor in shortest supply restricts the rate.

rubric.why: Increasing light intensity raises the rate until another factor becomes limiting.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of light intensity.
rubric.how: Award for relating light intensity to photosynthesis rate, including a plateau when another factor limits it.

rubric.why: Carbon dioxide is a raw material for photosynthesis, so its concentration can limit the rate.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of carbon dioxide concentration.
rubric.how: Award for linking carbon dioxide availability with the rate of photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes, so temperature affects its rate.
rubric.description: Explains the effect of temperature.
rubric.how: Award for stating that temperature affects the rate, preferably through enzyme activity.

rubric.why: Other necessary conditions, such as water and chlorophyll, may also limit photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Identifies another limiting factor.
rubric.how: Award for naming water or chlorophyll as an additional factor that can limit photosynthesis.

written.text: What are plastids? Explain its types.
modelAnswer: Plastids are membrane-bound organelles found in plant cells.
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments and give colour to plant parts such as flowers and fruits.
Leucoplasts are colourless plastids that store food, such as starch, oils, or proteins.

rubric.why: Plastids are membrane-bound organelles found in plant cells.
rubric.description: Defines plastids.
rubric.how: Award for identifying plastids as organelles in plant cells, preferably noting their membrane-bound structure.

rubric.why: Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis.
rubric.description: Explains chloroplasts.
rubric.how: Award for naming chloroplasts and linking them to photosynthesis.

rubric.why: Chromoplasts contain coloured pigments that give colour to plant parts.
rubric.description: Explains chromoplasts.
rubric.how: Award for identifying chromoplasts as pigment-containing plastids that impart colour.

rubric.why: Leucoplasts are colourless plastids commonly involved in food storage.
rubric.description: Explains leucoplasts.
rubric.how: Award for stating that leucoplasts are colourless and/or store food.

written.text: How small intestine helps the human body to digest food?
modelAnswer: In the small intestine, pancreatic juice supplies enzymes that digest carbohydrates, proteins, and fats.
Bile from the liver neutralizes acidic food arriving from the stomach and emulsifies fats into small droplets.
Enzymes in the intestinal juice complete the digestion of food into simple, soluble molecules.
The inner surface has many villi, which provide a large surface area for absorption.
Glucose and amino acids pass into the blood, while many products of fat digestion enter the lacteals.

rubric.why: Pancreatic juice enters the small intestine and provides enzymes for digestion.
rubric.description: Describes the role of pancreatic juice.
rubric.how: Award for stating that pancreatic enzymes act in the small intestine to digest food.

rubric.why: Bile helps make the conditions suitable for intestinal enzymes and emulsifies fats.
rubric.description: Describes the role of bile.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that bile neutralizes acidic chyme or emulsifies fats.

rubric.why: Intestinal enzymes complete the digestion of food molecules.
rubric.description: Explains completion of digestion.
rubric.how: Award for stating that intestinal juice or its enzymes complete digestion.

rubric.why: Villi increase the surface area for absorption of digested nutrients.
rubric.description: Explains absorption by villi.
rubric.how: Award for linking villi to absorption of digested food.

rubric.why: Digested nutrients pass into the blood, while many fats enter lacteals.
rubric.description: States where absorbed food goes.
